entry.title: Boulder: November 12, 2026 Boulder City Council Special Meeting
entry.content:
The council approved a consent agenda including an emergency ordinance raising the recreational marijuana sales tax from 3.5% to 5.5% effective January 1, 2027, then unanimously annexed a 5.43-acre Cherryville Road property with RR2 zoning and a Neighborhood One land use change. It unanimously adopted the rezoning of 3550 and 3850 Frontier Avenue to MU4 with a 3.5 FAR and 55-foot height allowance for a planned arts-centered mixed-use project, and approved by a 5-3 vote a non-conforming use expansion for a duplex at 969 10th Street. Council also directed staff to research legal options for University Hill compliance and to prepare options for an independent performance audit function.

Most discussed: Zoning, Housing, Development projects, University & students, Budget, Arts, culture & libraries

  • Emergency Ordinance Raising Recreational Marijuana Sales Tax: Council added an item to the agenda to adopt emergency ordinance 8791, which raises the additional recreational marijuana sales tax from 3.5% to 5.5%. The change was included in the 2027 budget after three budget sessions. Staff said it was brought as an emergency to meet the 45-day notice requirement to the Colorado Department of Revenue for a January 1 effective date. The consent agenda, including this item, was approved unanimously.
  • Cherryville Road Annexation and Initial Zoning: Council held a public hearing on annexing approximately 5.43 acres at 1275 Cherryville Road and 5995 Maxwell Lane. Staff explained that the Boulder Valley Comprehensive Plan update required a concurrent land use change from rural lands to Neighborhood One before annexation. The planning board had unanimously recommended the change, and the site would receive RR2 zoning. Council unanimously approved the land use map change, resolution 1384, and ordinance 8764 after no members of the public signed up to speak.
  • Frontier Avenue Rezoning to MU4 (Pearl Arts District): Council considered second reading of ordinance 8782 to rezone about 14.84 acres at 3550 and 3850 Frontier Avenue from industrial zoning to MU4, with amendments allowing a 3.5 FAR and 55-foot height for the future site review. Staff said the change was needed to match the regional hub land use designation and the TVAP Phase 2 vision. The applicant described a project with a performing arts venue, rehearsal space, housing, and a hotel, and asked council not to adopt two planning board amendments. Council unanimously adopted the ordinance as drafted by staff.
  • Non-Conforming Use Review at 969 10th Street: Council held a quasi-judicial public hearing on a non-conforming use review to convert attic space into habitable area and add one bedroom to each unit of an existing duplex in the RL1 zone, with no exterior expansion. Staff found the criteria met with conditions, including a declaration of use and bike storage. Several council members raised concerns about occupancy, wildfire evacuation, and neighborhood impacts, though staff noted occupancy is not a regulated criterion. Council approved the application by a 5-3 vote.
  • University Hill Legal Research Request: Council member Tara Shuart requested direction for legal research and policy alternatives on University Hill compliance and the effects of the family-friendly vibrant neighborhoods ordinance. The city attorney said the request was too broad and that staff needed specific questions. Council agreed to withdraw the item for now and return with a narrower request at a future meeting.
  • Independent Performance Audit Function: Council member Rob Spear requested direction for staff to research options for an independent performance audit function, including elected, council-appointed, contracted, or shared models, with costs and charter implications. Staff said they already had internal capacity for performance audits and agreed to provide options. Council members discussed whether the item should be a council priority and what problem an auditor would solve. Council voted 6 to 2 to direct staff to begin the research.

entry.title: Boulder: October 22, 2026 City Council Study Session
entry.content:
Council received a bike security and theft reduction update showing a 14% year-over-year drop in stolen bikes and a 13% recovery rate, with council raising staffing concerns and suggesting shop and e-bike measures. Council then reviewed the Wildfire Ready 2030 framework, including the WUI Risk Index, Home Hardening Implementation Hub, 14 performance measures, and roughly $1.85 million in proposed 2027 enhancements, and gave feedback to staff, who will return with a progress update in spring 2027. No formal votes were taken.

Most discussed: Wildfire, Housing, Council governance, Crime & justice, Bikes & pedestrians, Fire & EMS

  • Bike Security and Theft Reduction Update: Staff from Transportation and Mobility and the Boulder Police Department presented the completed council priority on bike theft, using a problem-oriented policing approach focused on registration via Bike Index, proper locking, bike parking improvements, and data-driven targeted operations. Staff reported a 14% year-over-year drop in thefts and a 13% recovery rate so far in 2026, on track to meet the 10% goals. Council members asked for full-year data, raised concerns about police understaffing and sustaining the work into 2027, and discussed e-bike targeting, shop registration defaults, and secure bike cages. Staff said the work will continue through ongoing education and communications.
  • Wildfire Ready 2030 Framework Overview: Fire Chief Calderazzo and Open Space and Mountain Parks staff introduced the Wildfire Ready 2030 initiative, which consolidates 137 projects into four strategies, 25 programs, and 10 tier-one priorities with life safety as the North Star. Staff described a 14-measure tracking system with 2030 targets, including 55% detailed home assessments and 20% home hardening in priority sections. The framework sets a 4-year window aligned with the Community Wildfire Protection Plan update. Tier-one program investments total over $10 million for the current year.
  • Home Hardening Implementation Hub: Staff presented the newly launched Wildfire Ready Action Hub, designed to help residents understand their property-level risk, find practical projects, and access financial resources without requiring a detailed home assessment. The hub is organized around resident goals rather than departments and includes a Headwaters Economics cost calculator. Council asked whether it links to GIS risk maps and whether the risk index could appear in property searches; staff said they would take those suggestions back.
  • WUI Risk Index and Geographic Prioritization: Open Space staff presented the Wildland Urban Interface Risk Index, which divides the western WUI into 12 sections ranked as highest, very high, or high risk based on likelihood, intensity, exposure, and susceptibility factors. Staff explained that the index guides prioritization of fuels management, home assessments, grant awards, and evacuation planning, and will support measurable targets. Council members asked about fuel prescriptions for dead and down material and generally supported using the index to focus resources.
  • Evacuation, Alerts, and Recovery Planning: Council asked how residents would receive evacuation information if cell service or power fails, and how schools in the WUI would coordinate with parents and the district. Emergency management staff described multiple alert channels, including radio, television, sirens, and door-to-door outreach, and noted ongoing work with cell carriers and the school district. Council also asked about recovery and relocation planning after events like the Marshall Fire, and staff described the progression from emergency shelter to disaster assistance and longer-term housing.
  • Home Hardening Standards and Contractor Ecosystem: Council members asked how the city could help residents move from assessments to completed hardening work, including contractor training, quality standards, and financing, drawing parallels to the Energy Smart concierge model. Staff said the city cannot endorse specific contractors but will expand training and coordinate neighborhood-scale work. Council also asked about reconciling the WOOEE building code with the IBHS standard used for existing-home assessments; staff said the two are not mutually exclusive and will crosswalk them, reporting back if policy changes are needed.
  • Hardening Targets and Aspirations: Council members debated whether the 20% home hardening and 55% detailed home assessment targets are ambitious enough, with several proposing a 100% assessment goal in the highest-risk zones and risk-tiered targets. Staff said targets were set based on current resources and participation but could be raised if capacity allows, and noted the 100% aspiration requires policy tools such as a mandatory hardening ordinance. Council members flagged the need for clarity on what a mandatory approach would require.
  • Rental Licenses, Policy Pathways, and Priorities: Council discussed tying rental license requirements to wildfire hardening, noting the city already uses this approach for Smart Regs, and asked how such ideas move from advice to direction. Staff explained that items needing council direction should come forward as a formal request, while others can be researched first. Council debated how to prioritize among many suggestions, and staff said the executive team would consider which actions offer the highest impact with available resources.
  • 2027 Priority Enhancements and Funding: Assistant City Manager Pam Davis presented four 2027 enhancement areas: home hardening grants and contractor training, community emergency preparedness, wildland fuels management, and tactical evacuation including siren upgrades. Staff described roughly $1.4 million already in the approved 2027 budget and about $1.85 million more from pending grants ($1.25 million) and a $600,000 open space fund realignment. The team also noted a possible $10 million Community Wildfire Defense Grant for 2028. Council members generally supported the approach and suggested possible additions such as volunteer debris work, neighborhood coordination, and a realtor disclosure partnership, with the realignment to return in December or spring.

entry.title: Boulder: October 1, 2026 - City of Boulder City Council Regular Meeting with 2027 Budget Public Hearing
entry.content:
Council heard extensive open comment on CU South, parks, the Boulderthon, cell towers and other issues, then approved the consent agenda and let the Nuropa campus site review proceed without a call-up. After a public hearing on the 2027 recommended budget, council passed budget ordinances 8777 through 8780 on first reading, but a straw poll left wildfire funding changes to be decided at an October 22 study session. Council also straw-polled unanimous support for staff to prepare a resolution backing the Front Range passenger rail sales tax measure.

Most discussed: Budget, Wildfire, Public comment, Taxes & fees, Open space, Parks & recreation

  • Open Public Comment: Nineteen residents signed up to speak on topics including a proposed tenants union, the Boulderthon road closures, small cell tower construction, CU South closure and flood risk, Gunbarrel parks, Spruce Pool, and Israel and Palestine. Several speakers criticized council and staff, and some comments drew a rebuke from council members as antisemitic. Staff responded afterward, promising follow-up on tenant resources, the Belmont site, small cell rules, event impacts and investment policy. Utilities Director Joe Taduchi then described the CU South fence and closure schedule.
  • Agenda Amendment and Consent Agenda: Council voted to add item 8A, the Front Range passenger rail sales tax discussion, to the agenda. Later, council approved consent agenda items 3A through 3H by unanimous roll call vote. These are procedural actions with no substantive policy debate.
  • Nuropa Campus Site Review Call-Up Check-In: Staff presented a site review application to redevelop the Nuropa campus on Arapahoe Avenue with about 135 residential units and a height modification to 55 feet. Council Member Winer raised shadow and setback concerns on Marine Street, and the applicant said the building sits about 40 to 50 feet from neighboring properties and that solar shadow standards were met. Council members said they would not call the item up, noting the preserved champion trees and historic Lincoln Hall.
  • CU South Project Closure and Cost: Utilities Director Joe Taduchi explained the public notice given for the CU South closure and the fencing plan, with a portion of the western edge remaining accessible. Council Member Nicole asked about litigation-related delays, and staff said the project estimate rose from about 61 million dollars in bids to 76 million after the financing plan changed to cash funding. Staff said utility rates would still stay on the planned path, though the claimed nine dollar monthly increase was not accurate.
  • 2027 Budget Presentation and Council Questions: Budget Officer Charlotte Husky presented the 2027 recommended budget of 552.6 million dollars, with an operating budget of 417.2 million dollars and a capital budget of 135.4 million dollars. Key highlights included about 10.9 million dollars for wildfire, three new police lieutenants, affordable housing investments, and a one-time funding bridge for Spruce Pool operations. Council asked about Sundance Festival costs, the Office of Customer Experience, agricultural plan updates, and whether the 6.3 million dollar general fund gap was fully closed, and staff confirmed the budget was balanced.
  • Public Hearing and Adoption of 2027 Budget Ordinances: Ten people signed up for the budget public hearing, with speakers focused on Spruce Pool, the East Boulder Rec Center, a proposed botanic garden at Hogan Pancost, the Boulder Chamber's views on economic vitality, and the Parks and Recreation Advisory Board's objections to proposed cuts. After the hearing, council members discussed trade-offs and the timing of wildfire decisions, and several members said the budget process needs to move earlier. Council adopted Ordinance 8777 on the budget with a 7 to 1 vote, and Ordinances 8778 and 8779 passed unanimously, while Ordinance 8780 changing fees and taxes passed 7 to 1.
  • Wildfire Resilience Funding Debate: Council discussed whether to set aside money now for wildfire mitigation, ahead of the October 22 study session where staff will present prioritized program areas and metrics. Council Member Benjamin proposed holding about 2.5 to 4 million dollars, and Council Member Kaplan proposed holding 600,000 dollars for mitigation crews and equipment. Staff said the realignment could come from open space capital projects, reserves or other funds, while community members have strongly opposed using open space funds for other purposes. Straw polls did not reach a majority for either option or for an alternative approach, so the status quo was retained and the decision was deferred until after October 22.
  • Spruce Pool and Parks Funding: Parks and Recreation Director Ally Rhodess said the Parks and Recreation Advisory Board did not recommend the budget because of recreation service cuts. The 2027 budget funds Spruce Pool operations with one-time dollars through 2027, and staff said it would return to council on the pool's operations in 2028. Several residents, including senior advocates, urged council to keep the pool open and find new revenue. Council members said they expected to find ongoing funding for Spruce Pool in future budgets.
  • Front Range Passenger Rail Sales Tax Measure: Council took up item 8A, a discussion of whether to support the Front Range passenger rail sales tax measure that would fund the Front Range train from Fort Collins through Boulder to Denver and Pueblo. The sponsoring council member asked for a straw poll on whether the city should take a formal position of support. Council voted unanimously in the straw poll, directing staff to prepare a resolution of support for a future business meeting.

entry.title: Boulder: September 24, 2026 City of Boulder City Council Study Session
entry.content:
Council received a public safety update covering policing, police oversight, and the municipal court, with staff reporting on officer staffing, crime trends, the new public safety information center, and court outcomes for unhoused and young adult cases. Council then reviewed a preliminary framework to update the sister cities resolution, and members supported a council committee to oversee sister city relationships with staff to bring a formal resolution back at a future meeting.

Most discussed: Police, Regional & state relations, Council governance, Crime & justice, Surveillance & privacy, Homelessness

  • Police Staffing and Retention: Chief Redford reported authorization for 190 sworn officers with 12 vacancies and about 30 positions not deployable as solo officers due to recruits, academy, or injury leave. Dispatcher and records staffing were also discussed, with recruiting underway. Officer departures since 2021 and the young workforce were highlighted, with exit interviews citing cost of living, out-of-state opportunities, and the aging police building. Council asked what would help retain officers, and the chief cited union contract progress and public support.
  • Public Safety Information Center and Community Connect Cameras: The chief introduced the new public safety information center, which consolidates technology and emergency monitoring and will be used for events and drone response. A council member asked how the voluntary Boulder Community Connect program lets residents share private camera feeds with police. The chief explained that feeds are viewed only when responding to calls, helping verify alarms and scale response. Privacy concerns were acknowledged, and the program was described as strictly opt-in.
  • Crime Trends and Proactive Policing: Chief Redford reported decreases in property crime, including burglary, auto theft, and bike theft, and lower person crimes except assaults, which are rising. Proactive activity such as directed patrols, pedestrian contacts, and traffic stops is up compared with the three-year average while calls for service are down but more complex. Drug-related charges are up, especially downtown, and a bike theft study session is planned for October. Officers are also focusing on alcohol enforcement and underage drinking.
  • Significant Incidents, Assaults, and Overdoses: Staff described a rise in financial crimes targeting vulnerable residents, with the Postal Inspector and other partners involved. Examples of serious assaults were presented, including an attempted murder case on Pearl Street where a drone helped locate the suspect. Officer assaults, including a choking incident that left an officer on injury leave, were discussed with credit to the District Attorney. Fatal overdoses, around 20 to 30 per year, were addressed through a drug task force case charging a dealer who supplied the fatal dose.
  • Community Engagement, Feedback, and Town Halls: The chief described liaison groups for many community segments, Spanish-speaking outreach, and events such as an ice cream truck engagement and National Night Out. Post-contact surveys sent to over 6,500 people showed 85 percent satisfaction with police service. Police chief town halls were held in South, East, and downtown Boulder, with a North Boulder town hall scheduled and one requested for the hill. A monthly newsletter and public crime dashboards were promoted.
  • Council Questions on Drug Use, Care Team, and Data Requests: Council asked about public drug use involving children and what can be done, and the chief noted state law changes that moved public drug possession from arrest to summons and jail limits. The high utilizers program and municipal court escalation were described as tools. Questions about the CARE team were answered by staff, who said the non-police response program lost a fire-based position and now operates with fewer clinicians. A council member requested race-disaggregated stop data and CARE outcome data, which staff agreed to provide.
  • E-Motos and Youth Traffic Safety: A council member raised injuries to young people riding e-motos without helmets on bike paths and roads. Staff explained that many so-called e-bikes are legally motorcycles requiring plates and licenses, and that parents often buy them unaware. Education efforts include bike rack tags, bike shop outreach, and traffic unit enforcement, along with officers on e-bikes. Staff clarified that officers typically issue citations or provide education, with courts deciding accountability, and documentation is logged in the system.
  • Police Oversight Update and Five-Year Review: Independent Police Monitor Sherri Dean and panel co-chairs reported on 2025 complaint data, including 149 allegations and 18 sustained findings, along with demographic trends and panel recruitment for the coming season. The co-chairs raised concerns that recent process changes have limited panel review to very few cases and reduced community complaint flow to the panel. A five-year review of the oversight system is underway with a consultant, and a report is expected in October with likely code changes. Council asked for data on officers who left in 2025 and whether they had complaints.
  • Municipal Court Presentation on Unhoused and Young Adult Cases: Presiding Judge Jeff Khan explained that municipal court handles lower-level offenses, while felonies and more serious charges go to state court. He reviewed camping and obstructing government operations cases, community court dismissals, counseling sessions, and warrant and in-custody hearing trends. Young adult case data covered minor in possession, nuisance party, fireworks, and fraudulent ID charges, with outcomes like deferred prosecutions and restorative justice. Council members raised concerns about large amplified parties near CU and asked about enforcement consistency and comparisons with other case types.
  • Sister Cities Resolution and Process Update: Assistant City Manager Pam Davis introduced a project to update Resolution 631 and clarify sister city application, review, reporting, and deactivation processes. The city clerk team reported on research from other cities, which found no dedicated staff or funding and identified needs for an online application, review timelines, and a deactivation process. Staff recommended five changes, and council supported a council committee of two members to oversee relationships, annual reporting, and possible cap or sunset criteria. Council gave non-binding direction, with staff to bring a revised resolution to a future meeting.

entry.title: Boulder: September 17, 2026 - Regular City Council Meeting
entry.content:
The council heard extensive open comment on the Panka Place street vacation, BBSD school closures, the CU South full closure for flood mitigation, and the Glenn Huntington Bandshell seating, then approved the consent agenda including the Panka Place vacation. Council also called up the bandshell landmark alteration for another review, adopted landmark designations for the Bird Stova House and the Hailman Bedell Stanic property, and repealed cannabis cultivation energy offset requirements.

Most discussed: Historic preservation, Development projects, Regional & state relations, Parks & recreation, Transportation, Human services

  • Panka Place Street Vacation for Fraser Expansion: Fraser residents and neighbors spoke in favor of vacating Panka Place, arguing it would create a safer shared street while keeping through access for emergency vehicles and pedestrians. Opponents and supporters debated traffic, walkability, and the church's parking lot. The council approved the vacation as part of the consent agenda.
  • BBSD School Closures and Council Role: Residents urged council to press the Boulder Valley School District to pause proposed elementary school closures, citing neighborhood cohesion, declining enrollment drivers, and the new comprehensive plan. Staff said the district makes the final decision and that the city has been coordinating with it on future school site uses. Council members Tisha Adams and Matt Benjamin said they would send letters asking for answers and more time.
  • CU South Full Closure for Flood Mitigation: Speakers asked the council to allow partial public access to the CU South open space during flood mitigation construction, noting the annexation agreement's recreation access provision and the 119 acres to become permanent open space. Speakers also questioned the flood mitigation design, cost, and lack of independent peer review. Staff said phasing was not feasible and that alternative recreation sites and FAQs would be provided.
  • Glenn Huntington Bandshell Landmark Alteration Call-Up: Speakers opposed the Parks Department proposal to demolish the bandshell seating, arguing it would harm a city landmark, add concrete and lawn maintenance costs, and create lingering issues. Council voted to call up the landmark alteration certificate application for another review. The vote to call it up passed.
  • Landmark Designations: Bird Stova House and Hailman Bedell Stanic Property: Staff presented two University Hill landmark designations recommended unanimously by the Landmarks Board. The Bird Stova House at 1004 Lincoln Place is a Craftsman and Tudor Revival home tied to the Stova family's long stewardship, and the Hailman Bedell Stanic property at 844-850 12th Street includes a southwest Mediterranean house by architect David Hull Holmes. Council adopted both ordinances unanimously after public hearings.
  • Repeal of Cannabis Cultivation Energy Offset Requirements: Staff recommended repealing energy offset requirements for marijuana cultivators because cultivation has declined from about 44 businesses to nine and the city struggled to collect impact fees. Advisory boards supported the change and staff said it would pursue industry-neutral building performance approaches later. A public speaker opposed the repeal, and council adopted Ordinance 8770 unanimously.
  • Declarations: Little League, Welcoming Week, and UN International Day of Peace: Council read a declaration honoring the South Boulder Little League 11U All-Star state champions. Council then recognized Welcoming Week, with Intercomo CEO John Lopez speaking about adult English learning programs. Council also proclaimed September 21, 2026 as the UN International Day of Peace.
  • Consent Agenda with Contested Items: Council approved the consent agenda items 4A through 4G, including the FAA airport grant and a resolution on the county commissioner seat reorganization. Council members Ryan Shuhart, Nicole Spear, Matt Benjamin, and others voted no or abstained on items D and F. The consent agenda was approved unanimously with noted exceptions.
  • Grant Place Student Density and Wildfire Risk: Alicia Curtain described a proposed 13-bedroom student duplex near Grant Place and raised wildfire risk concerns for the University Hill area. Council members asked staff about the status of the Grant Place request and about wildfire evacuation impacts. Council also discussed concerns over stealth dorms and the need to review the outcomes of the family-focused ordinance.

entry.title: Boulder: September 10, 2026 - City of Boulder City Council Study Session (2027 Recommended Budget)
entry.content:
Council held a study session on the city manager's 2027 recommended budget, totaling $552.6 million across all funds with a $412-417 million operating budget and $135.4 million capital budget, reflecting a second-slowest growth rate since the pandemic and continued reductions. Staff walked through revenue assumptions, goal-area changes, the six-year CIP including wildfire, fire station, and facilities projects, and the long-term financial strategy, then answered council questions on Alpine Balsam oversight, reserves, the auditor function, snow and ice removal, photo enforcement, and possible wildfire funding increases. No formal budget changes were adopted; council members were directed to submit any substantive amendments with identified offsets to the hotline by September 28 ahead of the October 1 first reading.

Most discussed: Budget, Council governance, Elections & ballot measures, Parks & recreation, Wildfire, Affordable housing

  • Budget Overview and Revenue Assumptions: Staff presented the 2027 recommended budget as balanced, with a $6.3 million general fund gap closed through ongoing reductions, realignments, and limited enhancements. Revenues are growing slowly, with sales and use tax up 3.3% and property tax up 6% after state legislation lowered assessed values. New revenue includes a transportation maintenance fee estimated at $3 million and a recreational marijuana tax increase from 3.5% to 5.5%. Utility rates rise 5% for water, 7% for wastewater, and 7% for stormwater.
  • Fund Our Future Community Engagement: Staff summarized feedback from over 500 community members collected through in-person and online conversations on service trade-offs across 25 services in 12 categories. Top community priorities were wildfire resilience, municipal infrastructure and facilities maintenance, public safety, and affordable housing. Staff said this input was a key pillar for budget decisions.
  • Goal-Area Operating Budget Changes: Scott Carpenter outlined changes by sustainability, equity, and resilience goal area. Notable items include $4.3 million for facilities maintenance, $11 million in total wildfire spending with a $300,000 climate-fund boost, three new police lieutenant positions, and $5.3 million for the Alpine Balsam affordable housing project. Reductions include Spruce Pool operations, East Boulder child watch services, and a $38,000 cut to microloan and rebate programs. The budget also funds the downtown ambassador program at $500,000 and a new community survey at $150,000.
  • Six-Year Capital Improvement Program: Charlotte Husky presented the 2027 to 2032 CIP totaling $827.7 million, with about 75% directed to utilities and transportation. Key projects include a $13.5 million Barker gravity pipeline repair, Colorado 119 bus priority signal improvements, and $31.7 million to replace Fire Stations 2 and 4. Wildfire mitigation projects on open space total about $1.7 million for the OSP climate and wildfire plan, along with fuels and grazing projects. Facilities maintenance includes $27.9 million in new projects funded by the CCRS tax.
  • Long-Term Financial Strategy and Next Steps: Staff described the long-term financial strategy, a comprehensive plan due in December, and ongoing structural issues tied to sales tax dependence and restricted revenues. Council was reminded that first reading is October 1 and adoption is October 15, with budget amendments due to the hotline by September 28 and required to include an identified offset. The recreational marijuana tax and several fee increases are part of the alternative funding mechanisms.
  • Alpine Balsam Project Oversight and Reporting: Council members Kaplan and Robin asked how cost overruns and project updates are communicated to council and the public. Staff said the project remains within council-approved budgets across its 11-year history and that a story map and project page were published. Staff acknowledged the need for more detail on major projects and said financial systems could better tag cross-departmental work.
  • Reserves and Facility Replacement Funding: Council asked whether reserves are set aside for facility replacement. Staff explained that a 2% current replacement value set-aside for buildings has been in place since facility strategic plan approval and is growing in the budget. Facilities staff clarified it funds ongoing replacement of building components, not wholesale rebuilding. Council members also asked about the 2026 bond and what happens to priority buildings if it fails.
  • Staffing and Fixed-Term Positions: Council asked how fixed-term and one-time-funded positions will be sustained in future years. Staff said some have multi-year funding while others are reviewed annually against criticality. Council also raised the property tax outlook, and staff said no further legislative assessment cuts are expected, with about a 5% increase assumed per reassessment cycle.
  • Tiered Services Framework and Priority Alignment: Nuria Rivera-Vandermark explained a new service tier framework: critically vital, federal and state mandated, city-mandated, strategic priority, and community enrichment. Council members asked why community-identified top priorities such as wildfire, snow and ice, public safety, and homelessness were not budgeted more clearly. Staff pointed to specific amounts for wildfire, facilities, police lieutenants, and affordable housing, and a council member said the spread was hard to track.
  • Spruce Pool, Silver Sneakers, and Pool Funding: Council members questioned the Spruce Pool reduction and whether revenue from Silver Sneakers or sugar-sweetened beverage tax funds could keep it open. Staff explained that the sugar-sweetened beverage tax has voter-approved uses tied to health equity, and that many facility costs are outpacing revenue. Parks and recreation said senior discount structures will be reviewed in its 2027 work plan.
  • Auditor Function and Process: Council discussed requests for an external performance auditor. Staff said the city has an internal auditor who can conduct performance audits and an external financial auditor selected by council. The internal audit committee screens community requests, and a public audit idea submission page was recently launched. Council agreed to schedule a future discussion on auditing in general.
  • Snow and Ice Removal Program: Council member Winer asked whether west-side streets with senior residents will be added to snow and ice removal. Transportation staff said the extra funding supports weather diagnostic units but does not add streets this season, since last winter was mild and the program needs another season to evaluate. A packet on program changes will come to council within the next month.
  • Photo Enforcement Van Elimination: Council asked why photo enforcement vans are being eliminated. Staff said costs outpaced revenue and that traffic patrol resources can respond instead. The police chief said neighborhoods with complaints will be prioritized, with motorcycle or car patrols, and the change will be monitored for any uptick in problems.
  • Wildfire Funding Recommendations and Grants: Council member Benjamin proposed roughly $2 million in added climate initiative funding, $4 to 5 million in open space fuels management, and $2 to 3 million from new grants to expand wildfire mitigation. Other council members said the proposal was too large a climate cut and that it needed further staff review and a hotline submission. Staff noted wildfire grants total $2.2 million across five awards and that competitive grants are pursued selectively.
  • Policy Alignment and Community Connectors: Council member Tina argued that budget reallocations at the end of the process bypass policy work, and that changes should come through adopted policy. Council member Adams raised concerns about nuisance enforcement on the Hill, San Lazaro annexation support, and cuts to the community connectors outreach component. Staff said these items would be reviewed or handled through separate appropriations, and that the funding question for outreach would be answered later.
  • Energy Costs, Evacuation Planning, and Water Supply: Council member Adams questioned whether the budget accounts for rising energy and fuel costs, evacuation and recovery costs after wildfire, and water supply scenarios. Staff said capital project managers include energy costs in their projections and that the formula would be provided. Adams said these concerns would be submitted through the hotline.

entry.title: Boulder: September 3, 2026 City of Boulder City Council Special Meeting and Regular Meeting
entry.content:
The council convened a special meeting to enter executive session for confidential legal advice on authorized uses of city open space, then held its regular meeting with extensive public comment on the Frasier Meadows expansion and Panka Place vacation, BVSD school closures, and Spruce Pool funding. The council approved the consent agenda except item 4E, adopted pedal cab licensing ordinance 8757 unanimously, received updates on state housing laws, and directed staff to proceed with a small business and restaurant task force concept and a council position supporting the Boulder County five-commissioner ballot measure.

Most discussed: Legal & litigation, Open space, Zoning, Development projects, Public comment, Regional & state relations

  • Special meeting and executive session: The council convened its special meeting and voted unanimously to enter executive session to receive confidential legal advice on authorized uses of city open space. After returning to public session, the council confirmed the participants and concluded the executive session with no reported improper action.
  • Frasier Meadows expansion and Panka Place vacation public comment: Numerous residents spoke against the Frasier Meadows senior living expansion, citing a 55-foot height modification, inadequate transitions to single-family homes, traffic and construction concerns, and the lack of affordable units. Many urged the council to call up the project for a public hearing and to avoid giving Panka Place to the applicant, as it serves as an emergency and evacuation route. Supporters of senior housing also spoke, while residents raised questions about the loss of a public connection.
  • BVSD neighborhood school closures: Residents and a young student spoke against the proposed BVSD closure of neighborhood schools, including Flat Irons Elementary, arguing it conflicts with city planning goals for walkable neighborhoods and increases traffic and emissions. Speakers asked the council to request that BVSD delay its vote for one year. The council acknowledged the concerns without taking formal action.
  • Spruce Pool funding and closure concerns: Swimmers and advocates spoke in favor of keeping Spruce Pool open, citing safety for older adults and people with disabilities, its role as an overflow pool, and its historic value. A speaker noted proposed cuts to Spruce and Scott pool funding for 2027 and no budgeted funding for 2028. Staff said funding is secured for one year and that Parks and Recreation will meet with supporters, and Council Member Brockett pledged to work on solutions.
  • Student rentals, party houses, and Grant Place densification: Residents of Grant Place and University Hill described a 12-bedroom student duplex built under the affordable housing zoning rules, along with party house problems, noise, and trash. Speakers asked the city to address stealth dorm expansion and consider impact fees on landlord-owned properties. Staff said the duplex met zoning and building code requirements and that a nuisance ordinance and enforcement process exist, with follow-up promised.
  • Other public comments on police, bears, and other issues: A resident described difficulties getting police to act on evidence related to identity theft and stalking and proposed new state evidence intake laws. Another resident spoke about bears in downtown Boulder and the city trash ordinance, while others addressed international issues. Staff said the police department would follow up on the evidence case.
  • Declaration honoring Mark Wallik: Council members read a declaration honoring former council member Mark Wallik for his seven years of service on council. Wallik responded with remarks on his time on council and his family support. The council recognized his contributions to public safety, housing, open space, and governance.
  • Pollinator Appreciation Month declaration: City staff and partners presented a new citywide bee biomonitoring initiative that uses honeybee hives and native bee homes to gather data on plant diversity and environmental contaminants. Council Member Shuhart read the declaration proclaiming September 2026 Pollinator Appreciation Month. A council member asked about expanding the program to northern areas, and staff said it will expand next year.
  • Consent agenda and city employee evaluations: The council discussed the consent agenda, including the 2025-26 performance evaluations and salary adjustments for the city manager, city attorney, and municipal court judge, all of which received top ratings. One council member voted against item 4E, citing concerns about the evaluation process, the consultant used, and public input. The consent agenda was approved 8 to 0 with one nay on item 4E.
  • Frasier Meadows call-up check-in: The council reviewed the site review amendment for the Frasier and Mountain View Methodist properties at 350 and 355 Panka Place, a 55-foot, 96-unit independent living building. Staff clarified public access easement conditions, flood review, inclusionary housing fees of about $9.4 million, and energy and solar requirements. A motion to call up the project failed for lack of a second.
  • Xcel Energy facility concept plan check-in: The council reviewed a concept plan to expand the Xcel Energy service and operations facility at 2655 North 63rd Street. Staff confirmed the project concerns existing operations and fleet maintenance, not the power plant or coal ash work. No council member requested a call-up.
  • Pedal cab agency and driver licensing ordinance 8757: Staff presented ordinance 8757 to create agency and driver licenses for pedal cabs, including insurance, background checks, fees to cover administrative costs, enforcement authority, and a ban on selling products while operating. Council asked about enforcement, minimum wage rules, sales tax, and how Denver handles licensing, and staff said there are no current local pedal cab agencies. The council adopted the ordinance unanimously 7 to 0 after a public hearing with no speakers.
  • State affordable housing fund (Proposition 123) update: Staff explained that Proposition 123 funding requires a 90-day fast-track review for affordable housing projects by year end to keep Boulder eligible. The proposal removes planning board call-ups and automatic hearings for site reviews with height modifications for projects with at least 50 percent affordable units. Council supported staff's approach and the planning board unanimously recommended it, with an ordinance expected in October and November.
  • Transit-oriented communities bill and Home Act updates: Staff described the state transit-oriented communities bill, which sets a housing opportunity goal of about 123,000 units for Boulder, and said current estimates show the city is close to meeting it with some code changes. Council supported removing call-ups for form-based code reviews and considering reduced ground-floor retail requirements. Staff also explained the Home Act's administrative review, height, and density standards for qualifying properties, with council giving a majority direction to pursue those changes.
  • Small business and restaurant task force concept: Council Members Matt and Ryan proposed forming a small informal working group of restaurant owners and worker representatives to build relationships and explore solutions for restaurants and workers. The group is not intended to be an official task force or to require staff time, and it may report recommendations before the 2027 council retreat. Council unanimously gave direction to proceed.
  • Boulder County five-commissioner ballot measure: Council Member Shuhart proposed that the city take a support position on the Boulder County ballot measure to expand the county commission from three to five members. Council members debated respecting county governance, the district map and representation impacts, and the county's ongoing partnership with the city. A straw poll gave council direction to take a support position, with a 5 to 3 vote.

entry.title: Boulder: August 27, 2026 - Boulder City Council Study Session
entry.content:
Council received an Xcel Energy partnership update covering wildfire mitigation, undergrounding, reliability, and emissions progress, then questioned Xcel on outages, rates, resilience hubs, and microgrids. Staff then presented a midyear progress check on the council-priority wildfire resilience project, including a home hardening hub and a prioritization framework with a WOOI risk index. No binding votes were taken; staff will return with follow-up responses and further materials in October.

Most discussed: Wildfire, Energy & utilities, Emergency management, Equity & civil rights, Budget, Zoning

  • Xcel Energy Partnership Update and Wildfire Mitigation Presentation: Xcel Energy leaders presented progress under the Boulder energy partnership agreement, including emissions reduction targets, coal retirements, and 2030 carbon-free goals. Xcel detailed its wildfire mitigation plan, including undergrounding of three feeders, a two-phase transmission rebuild, enhanced power line safety settings, AI cameras, and public safety power shutoff preparations. The presentation also covered 120 megawatts of planned capacity additions, a clean heat pilot with a June 2027 PUC filing, and a second voter report. Staff noted that Excel's outage and reliability work is being coordinated with city staff through a weekly meeting.
  • Energy Resilience Priority and Council Questions to Xcel: Staff introduced the energy resilience council priority and a set of questions on whether the partnership is delivering expected outcomes. Council pressed Xcel on rolling outages, market purchases and rate impacts, and the frequency and duration of outages in Boulder neighborhoods. Councilmembers asked about resilience hubs, community microgrids, a $10 million energy assistance commitment, billing and customer service issues tied to a PUC investigation, and whether the utility can provide a scorecard. Xcel committed to written follow-up on many questions, and council members were given one-minute closing comments.
  • Wildfire Resilience Priority: Home Hardening Implementation Hub: Staff provided a progress check on the wildfire resilience council priority, starting with an overview from the Office of Disaster Management on wildland urban interface conflagration risk and regional coordination. The team described a planned home hardening implementation hub with pathways for low-cost projects, cost estimates, insurance guidance, and neighbor engagement, with a soft launch planned for late September. Council discussed barriers such as finding qualified contractors, renter participation, and the need for trusted vetted resources. Staff noted that a local contractor list would need legal review to avoid implied endorsement.
  • Wildfire Mitigation Prioritization, WOOI Risk Index, and Council Discussion: Staff presented an inventory of about 137 wildfire projects organized into 25 programs, with 10 tier one programs identified through a survey of wildfire professionals. A draft WOOI risk index divided the western wildland urban interface into 12 sections, showing highest risk west of Broadway, and staff proposed 2030 measures and targets. Council asked about scenario planning under drier or hotter conditions, evacuation capacity, retroactive and mandatory home hardening, funding tradeoffs, revolving loan options, and how land use decisions interact with high-risk areas. Staff will bring the final risk index, refined measures, and a full study session in October.

entry.title: Boulder: August 20, 2026 - Regular City Council Meeting
entry.content:
The Boulder City Council held its regular meeting with extended open comment on topics including Gaza divestment, a hunting ballot measure, wildfire-zone development, and Flock license plate readers, followed by a consent agenda approving a $400 million bond ballot item and other items. Council unanimously adopted ordinances 8771 and 8772 authorizing property acquisition for the North and South 30th Street safety projects. The board of the Downtown Commercial District then approved the sale of the Spruce Street parking lot at 2121 Broadway to a hotel developer by a 7-1 vote after a lengthy public hearing.

Most discussed: Development projects, Public comment, Parking, Transportation, Economic development, Bikes & pedestrians

  • Open Public Comment: Residents spoke during open comment on Gaza and divestment, the Initiative 302 hunting amendment, a pause on high-density student housing in wildfire zones, and tax burdens. Council members and staff responded afterward, with staff noting a planned wildfire home-hardening presentation on August 27. Speakers were limited to two-minute time slots under the decorum rules read at the start.
  • Flock License Plate Reader Pause: Staff confirmed a pause on the automated license plate reader RFP and said the city will not sign a contract until a more detailed community engagement plan is in place. The existing cameras remain in use on a month-to-month basis with the current provider. Staff also said additional guardrails are being considered and will be shared in an upcoming press release.
  • Consent Agenda and Bond Ordinance 8758: Council approved consent agenda items 3A through 3C and 3E through 3J unanimously after a resident objected to the roughly $400 million bond ordinance. Council members discussed the need for budget transparency, the possibility of an independent auditor, and whether the bond would affect the graduated income tax. Staff explained the Alpine Balsam housing funds and said no affordable housing fund money is going to the Western City campus.
  • Call-Up Check-In and Suspension of Rules: Council did not call up item 4A, a landmark alteration certificate to relocate an accessory building at 1733 Canyon Boulevard. Council then voted unanimously to suspend procedural rules to allow three public hearings that evening.
  • North and South 30th Street Property Acquisition Ordinances: Staff requested authority to acquire easements along North 30th and South 30th Street by negotiation or eminent domain to protect federal grant spending deadlines. The North 30th project costs about $9.3 million, with roughly half of about 50 properties needing temporary or permanent easements averaging under 1,000 square feet. Council unanimously adopted Ordinance 8771 for North 30th and Ordinance 8772 for South 30th, and staff said South 30th construction would finish a year ahead of North 30th.
  • Spruce Street Parking Lot Sale: Staff Presentation and Questions: Staff presented an unsolicited offer from MALR Boulder LLC to buy the KGID-owned surface lot at 2121 Broadway for $5.8 million for a 110-room boutique hotel. The terms include six 30-year community benefit covenants covering affordable commercial space, public space, arts, contracting, energy performance, and alley access for First Congregational Church. A parking study found the 59 lost spaces could be absorbed by nearby garages, and council questioned water demand, Visit Boulder support, and the revenue impact on KGID.
  • Spruce Street Lot Public Hearing: Nineteen speakers addressed the proposed sale, and most opposing speakers were from First Congregational Church, Trinity Lutheran, and local businesses. Their main concerns were loss of accessible parking for elderly and disabled visitors, congestion, and the lack of community process before the sale. Supporters, including the developer, cited the vibrancy of the Ramble Hotel in Denver, economic benefits, and the need for more downtown lodging for Sundance.
  • Council Deliberation and Board Vote on Spruce Lot Sale: Council members said the sale would not approve the hotel design, since later site and concept review would still be required under normal development rules. Several members highlighted the long-term fiscal benefit of tax revenue from the hotel and the strength of the covenants, while others raised concerns about parking, water, and energy. The board then approved the purchase agreement by a 7-1 vote, with Council Member Adams voting no.

entry.title: Boulder: August 13 2026 City of Boulder City Council Special Meeting and Study Session
entry.content:
The council convened a special meeting and held an executive session to receive confidential legal advice on potential new litigation, approved unanimously. In the study session, staff previewed the 2027 through 2030 citywide strategic plan process and gathered council feedback, then presented goals for the Civic Area East Bookend development partnership RFP and asked for feedback before release. The council also gave staff non-binding direction to draft resolutions opposing several state ballot measures and supporting the county early childhood measure, the graduated income tax, and two others, with formal votes to follow at a later meeting.

Most discussed: Legal & litigation, Council governance, Development projects, Elections & ballot measures, Budget, Parks & recreation

  • Special Meeting and Executive Session on Potential Litigation: The council convened a special meeting and voted unanimously to enter executive session under Colorado law and the city charter to receive confidential legal advice on potential new litigation. Participants were listed for the record and no concerns about improper discussion were raised. The special meeting was then reconvened and closed at 6:01 p.m.
  • Strategic Plan 2027 to 2030 Check-In: Staff presented the process for developing the next four-year citywide strategic plan, including a world of possibilities document with about 41 inputs drawn from roughly 170 staff proposals. The presentation described a prioritization rubric, the relationship to the comprehensive plan and budget tiers, and a timeline with a community workshop on November 14 and a January pre-retreat study session. Council members raised concerns about council ownership of the process, access to budget versus actuals and prior plan outcomes, and the need for a clearer prioritization methodology. Members suggested adding items such as a Title 9 rewrite, a two-year budget process, and a category for services no longer core to the city's mission.
  • Civic Area East Bookend Development Partnership RFP: Staff presented the goals and process for a public-private development partnership on the city-owned East Bookend of the Civic Area, with an optional West Bookend, to deliver a year-round food destination with the Boulder County Farmers Market, arts and culture uses, and park connections. The RFI drew nine responses that broadly supported the partnership model, and the RFP is planned for late summer with a partner selected in early 2027. Council discussed selection committee membership, ground-floor commercial uses, developer experience, park safety and activation, ongoing park maintenance costs, phasing, and the Arboretum Path, which is currently outside the funded phase. Council members asked staff to make the community vision goals more explicit and to consider affordability, economic synergy with downtown, and total cost of ownership.
  • 2026 State and County Ballot Measure Positions: Staff explained that the city can take an official position on ballot measures only through a council-adopted resolution and asked whether council wanted drafts for any measures. The county early childhood care mill levy and several state measures were reviewed, including initiatives on fentanyl penalties, law enforcement reporting, sports participation, minors' surgeries, road funding, natural gas rights, and the graduated income tax. Council members gave straw-poll direction to draft non-binding resolutions opposing the fentanyl measure and the road funding measure, supporting the county child care measure, the graduated income tax, and Proposition NN, and supporting the sporting goods tax revenue for conservation measure only after further review. Formal votes on the resolutions are expected at a later regular meeting.

entry.title: Boulder: August 6, 2026 - Boulder City Council Regular Meeting
entry.content:
The council heard extensive open comment and staff presentations, then voted on five ordinances for the November 3, 2026 ballot. It unanimously referred the firefighter collective bargaining charter amendment (8761), the recreation and safety bond (8758, amended to name a lap pool), and the debt limit charter amendment (8762), and referred the residential vacancy excise tax (8759) by a 7-1 vote. The downtown development authority measure (8763) failed 4-4, and the council then directed staff to scope community engagement; the meeting ended by approving the Boulder Valley Comprehensive Plan update conditions and amendments.

Most discussed: Elections & ballot measures, Public comment, Economic development, Zoning, Open space, Labor & wages

  • Open Comment: Residents spoke on the Fort Chambers interpretive design, Sand Creek memorialization, Spruce Pool and South Boulder Rec Center, a shelter bathroom sanitation issue, HOA costs in permanently affordable homes, and Middle East policy. Staff responded that they would follow up with Right Relationship Boulder, Spruce Pool would close for renovations after Labor Day, and the shelter issue was being addressed with shelter leadership and public health. Council members raised tribal consultation timing, CU Boulder coordination, and the city's investment portfolio.
  • Consent Agenda and Call-Up Check-Ins: After reconvening at 6:30 p.m., the council passed the consent agenda items 3A through 3C by voice vote. Three outside city utility permit requests on Cherryville Road, Frying Pan Road, and Cottonwood Drive were not called up for discussion.
  • Recreation and Safety Bond Presentation and Debate: Staff presented a proposed 400 million dollar general obligation bond to fund replacing the South Boulder Rec Center, renovating North Boulder Rec Center and the West Senior Center, and building a public safety and 911 dispatch facility, along with fire station and municipal building work. Staff said the bond would address a backlog of facilities needs that developed over decades and cited a 6.5 million dollar projected 2027 general fund gap. Residents and council members pressed for binding ballot language guaranteeing the South Boulder Rec Center's core amenities, such as a lap pool and gym.
  • Debt Limit Charter Amendment: Staff explained that ordinance 8762 would change the city charter debt limit calculation from assessed value to actual value, bringing Boulder in line with other Boulder County communities and state statute. Council discussed the change as part of its long-term financial strategy. The council then approved the measure unanimously for the November ballot.
  • Residential Vacancy Excise Tax: Ordinance 8759 would impose an excise tax on homes occupied 183 days or fewer per year, starting January 1, 2028, at 4,000 dollars per unit with annual CPI adjustments up to a maximum of 7,000 dollars per unit. Supporters said it would encourage long-term rentals and help housing affordability, and staff said an implementing ordinance would address exemptions. Council member Nicole Speer opposed, arguing a fee would be a better approach, and the council referred it to the ballot 7-1.
  • Firefighter Collective Bargaining Charter Amendment: Ordinance 8761 would add a new charter section guaranteeing full-time fire department employees the right to bargain collectively, along with changes to the impasse procedure. The Boulder Association of Firefighters and city leadership reached agreement on the language, avoiding a petition effort. The council adopted the ordinance unanimously for the November ballot.
  • Downtown Development Authority Presentation and Council Questions: Staff presented the proposed downtown development authority covering downtown and University Hill, with tax increment financing projections, a draft letter of intent, and council oversight through appointments and budget approval. Staff said the DDA would be a separate entity, that roughly 2,200 qualified electors in the district would vote, and that the bond and DDA projections were separate from the city's citywide forecast. Council questions addressed sales tax base years, Sundance Film Festival timing, precedents from other Colorado DDAs, and whether water supply was included in long-term projections.
  • Public Hearing on Ballot Measures: More than 60 residents spoke, with strong opposition and support on the DDA, the rec center bond's lack of binding amenity language, and the vacancy tax. Speakers included library trustees requesting a board seat and an IGA, Downtown Boulder Partnership and Chamber representatives supporting the DDA, and Sierra Club and open space advocates raising concerns about dedicated tax revenue. Several speakers also opposed or supported the collective bargaining measure and questioned the bond's debt obligations.
  • Council Votes on Ballot Measures: The council unanimously adopted ordinance 8761 for firefighter collective bargaining and then approved ordinance 8758 unanimously after adding a lap pool to the South Boulder Rec Center language. Ordinance 8759 passed 7-1 with Council Member Spear opposed, and ordinance 8762 passed unanimously. Ordinance 8763 to form the DDA failed 4-4, and council gave staff direction to scope next steps and community engagement by a 6-0 show of hands.
  • Boulder Valley Comprehensive Plan Update: Staff presented remaining conditions of approval and recommended amendments from the planning board, county commissioners, and county planning commission. Council accepted staff's recommendation to approve the conditions and amendments, including the county's revised municipal airport policy, the removal of the history section, and the rural lands designation for area 2. A proposal to restore near-transit language for neighborhood one housing failed a straw poll, and all three motions passed unanimously.

entry.title: Boulder: July 30, 2026 - City of Boulder City Council Special Meeting
entry.content:
The council held a public hearing on second reading of Ordinance 8754 to amend the local minimum wage code and set a local tip offset amount for food and beverage workers, hearing extensive public testimony from workers, labor groups, restaurant representatives, and residents. After discussion, no motion was made to change the tip offset, so the existing minimum wage schedule will proceed unchanged, and council expressed support for a task force on restaurant sustainability. The meeting also addressed a direction request on a wildfire resilience open space measure, where council agreed to pursue an ordinance rather than a ballot measure and to hold an executive session on legal advice before proceeding.

Most discussed: Economic development, Public comment, Labor & wages, Council governance, Wildfire, Taxes & fees

  • Consent Agenda and Agenda Amendment: Council added item 4A to the agenda unanimously and then approved consent agenda items 2A and 2B by roll call vote.
  • Staff Presentation on Tip Offset Ordinance 8754: Staff presented the second reading of Ordinance 8754, explaining the tip offset mechanics, the 2026 offset of $3.20 and Colorado law allowing a local increase up to $4.68. Presenters reviewed restaurant industry sales tax, job, and visitation trends showing slowing growth. Community engagement results from about 280 questionnaire responses were summarized, followed by four options ranging from status quo to a temporary base wage freeze.
  • Council Questions on Restaurant Savings Messaging: Council member Matt questioned how the status quo option could be presented as $62,800 in restaurant savings, arguing it was misleading because it is not new money. Staff explained the figure reflects current savings from the existing $3.20 offset. Council member Tina asked whether the sales tax chart was inflation adjusted, and staff said it was not.
  • Public Hearing on Tip Offset: Public hearing testimony from roughly 28 signed-up speakers, with two-minute limits, featured workers, union organizers, students, and restaurant representatives. Most speakers urged council to keep the scheduled minimum wage increases and avoid expanding the tip offset, citing rents and cost of living. Speakers also proposed alternatives such as commercial vacancy taxes, rent relief, delivery fee caps, and a task force, while the Boulder Chamber and Colorado Restaurant Association urged policy relief for restaurants.
  • Council Deliberation and Task Force Support: Council members discussed the tension between supporting restaurants and protecting workers, with several calling for a collaborative task force including labor, business, landlords, and experts. Members expressed that the current schedule should stay in place, and no motion was made to change the tip offset. Council also discussed other levers such as power outage reduction, permitting efficiency, and fee structures.
  • Task Force Process Question: Council member Matt asked how quickly a restaurant and workforce task force could begin, and staff requested clarity on scope, leadership, and resources. The mayor suggested a future council action request with a specific proposal, and council member Nicole offered to convene informal discussions independently. The mayor confirmed that the task force would be brought back at a future meeting.
  • Agenda Item 4A: Wildfire Resilience Open Space Measure Direction: Staff from the city manager's office asked council for direction on whether to pursue a charter amendment ballot measure, a code change, or neither for wildfire resilience on open space. The Open Space Board of Trustees had recommended a charter amendment, while staff recommended a code change. Council indicated consensus against a ballot measure and in favor of an ordinance.
  • Executive Session and Process Concerns: Council agreed unanimously to hold an executive session to receive confidential legal advice before deciding on an ordinance. Council members raised concerns about late receipt of a confidential memo and that the Open Space Board did not receive the legal advice before voting. Staff committed to better timing and process going forward.

entry.title: Boulder: July 23, 2026 - City of Boulder City Council Special Meeting
entry.content:
The council amended its agenda, approved the consent agenda, and continued the Boulder Valley Comprehensive Plan adoption to August 6, 2026. After a long public hearing on the Boulder Municipal Airport's continued operation, the council voted 8-1 to approve continued indefinite operation with a condition that any FAA grant carrying perpetuity obligations come back to council for a vote before acceptance. Councilmember Wallik resigned from council at the end of the meeting.

Most discussed: Public comment, Council governance, Transportation, Budget, Legal & litigation, Public health

  • Roll Call and Agenda Amendment: The council took roll with all members present and a quorum established. The agenda was amended to continue item 3A (BVCP adoption) and add items 2E (special counsel appointment for code of conduct complaints) and 2F (holding the July 30 special meeting in person). The amendment passed unanimously.
  • Consent Agenda: The consent agenda (items 2A through 2F) was approved unanimously. Item 2E authorized the city attorney to appoint special counsel because the city attorney's office had a conflict in investigating a complaint against a board member under the code of conduct. Council also praised the firefighters union for progress on collective bargaining charter language for a future ballot.
  • Boulder Valley Comprehensive Plan Adoption Continued: Staff introduced the BVCP adoption, the first public hearing, and the four bodies reviewing it. Council agreed to open and continue the hearing because of limited time and high public interest. The item was continued to August 6, 2026, and the motion passed unanimously.
  • Airport Public Hearing Presentation: Transportation and Mobility staff presented updated financial scenarios for the Boulder Municipal Airport, including indefinite operation with and without FAA grants. Staff estimated a deficit of about $7 million to $26 million depending on the scenario and identified alternative revenue ideas such as landing fees, hangar development, and solar. Staff said no single alternative would close the gap, and that FAA grants carry perpetual obligations for land acquisition.
  • Council Questions to Staff and Special Counsel: Councilmembers asked about alternative financing, the near-term FAA grant deadlines, and whether the city could restrict noise. Special outside counsel explained federal obligations, FAA perpetuity conditions, and litigation risks and timelines, including Santa Monica's roughly 12-year dispute. Staff also noted the city's position in ongoing litigation that the perpetuity requirement does not apply.
  • Public Hearing on Airport Operations: Speakers were limited to two minutes each and roughly 70 people signed up. Supporters cited emergency medevac and firefighting uses, flight training and youth programs, research flights, economic impact, and the value of unleaded fuel and quieter aircraft. Opponents raised noise and lead concerns, land-use and perpetuity risks, the need for a public vote, and the view that landing fees and self-sustaining models were unexamined. Many speakers asked the council to put the question to voters.
  • Council Deliberation and Motions: Councilmembers discussed fiscal risk, deferred maintenance, long-term land value, climate and wildfire needs, and the value of aviation to the community. A motion by Councilmember Shuhart for a one-year waiting period on perpetuity-covenant obligations was defeated 6 to 3. A staff-recommended motion to approve continued operation was then amended by Councilmember Spear to require council approval of the next FAA grant with perpetuity obligations, and the amendment passed 6 to 3. The amended motion passed 8 to 1.
  • Councilmember Resignation: Councilmember Wallik made a personal privilege statement opposing the airport decision as a surrender of land in perpetuity and announced his immediate resignation from council. Other members expressed regret and thanked him for his service, and staff expressed their respect for his decision.
  • Adjournment: The mayor closed the meeting at 10:25 p.m. after the closing remarks and staff comments concluded.

entry.title: Boulder: June 25, 2026 - Boulder City Council Special Meeting
entry.content:
Council deliberated on the major update to the Boulder Valley Comprehensive Plan, straw-polling conditions of approval and recommended amendments from the Planning Board, County Planning Commission, and Board of County Commissioners, then approved the plan with those changes by unanimous motions, though it still needs further rounds of approval by the other bodies. Council also gave staff direction to develop a $400 million recreation and public safety bond and a vacancy excise tax for the November 2026 ballot, and heard results from the Fund Our Future community engagement.

Most discussed: Zoning, Housing, Affordable housing, Regional & state relations, Taxes & fees, Council governance

  • Staff overview of the plan approval process: Planning staff explained that the Boulder Valley Comprehensive Plan must be adopted in identical form by all four approving bodies, so this meeting was deliberation only with no public testimony. Staff outlined a series of motions and a likely second round of consideration in July and August. Staff noted the Planning Board and Board of County Commissioners conditions of approval are binding unless council agrees to them.
  • Conditions of approval from Planning Board and County Commissioners: Planning Board conditioned approval on changes to housing policy 82 and the municipal airport policy 79. The Board of County Commissioners proposed six conditions, including tribal consultation language, deleting four pages of planning history, and changing area two neighborhood one designations to rural. Staff recommended against most conditions but supported some language edits, and noted the county changes would need further review.
  • Recommended amendments from the four approval bodies: Staff reviewed 14 recommended amendments, including adding residential uses to the industrial designation, changing street and parks language, and redesignating several East Boulder parcels to Innovation and Production Hub or industrial. Staff opposed most map changes as inconsistent with the East Boulder Subcommunity Plan and unreviewed by the community. Staff supported several smaller edits, including county renewable energy and rural working lands language.
  • Council clarifying questions and deliberation: Council asked whether middle-income housing and attainable housing were adequately addressed, and whether affordability language could be used to limit housing near the airport. Staff explained that the policy emphasizes middle-income housing under policy 84 and that the airport lists are examples rather than mandates. Council members also questioned the removal of the planning history section and the climate and water priorities in the plan.
  • Straw poll on housing diversity and supply (policy 82): Council considered whether to keep the original policy 82 language or adopt Planning Board or County Commissioner edits that would emphasize more affordable housing and prioritize middle housing. Several members argued the county language was valuable because the county controls land that could be housed, but the mayor noted its rural proposal would discourage county housing. After successive straw polls, council kept the original language.
  • Straw poll on municipal airport language (policy 79): Council debated Planning Board revisions to the airport policy, which added noise management examples and ongoing county coordination. Matt Benjamin proposed a middle-ground version, but council members were split on whether the language was operational or aspirational. Following straw polls, council retained the original airport policy language.
  • Board of County Commissioners conditions straw polls: Council accepted county conditions to add county references and remove American Indian from policy 102, and to remove the word city from policy 103 to limit it to city action. Council rejected the proposal to delete the 50-year planning history pages after discussion about accuracy and the potential to revise later. Council also agreed to add federally before recognized tribes in a related policy, and voted to change only the Gunbarrel area two neighborhood one designations to rural rather than all of area two.
  • Straw polls on recommended amendments: Council straw polled staff and board recommended amendments one by one, asking first whether any member would advocate each change. Council approved Planning Board edits to the housing and transportation definitions, the parks and streets language, and the small houses on small lots language with multi-unit buildings near transit. Council rejected the 15-minute neighborhood monitoring language as operational and removed the proposed industrial residential map changes after straw polls.
  • Wildfire life safety and renewable energy amendments: Council Member Kaplan proposed adding language requiring a holistic wildfire risk approach, including emergency management and egress capacity, when evaluating density within mapped wildfire ignition zones. Staff suggested it could fit better as an example in the natural hazards section, and council adopted it as a recommendation. Council also approved adding renewable before energy in local energy generation policy 53 and accepted the county's emergency utility services language in policy 16.
  • Motions to approve the comprehensive plan: Council adopted four motions to approve the major update, approving the plan with the Board of County Commissioners conditions, the recommended amendments, and council conditions, all as indicated by the straw polls. Each motion passed unanimously on roll call. The mayor noted the process is not complete because the other approval bodies must still act.
  • Ballot measure direction for city facilities: Staff presented polling results showing that a $400 million recreation and safety bond polled better than a $200 million option, though neither reached a majority on its own. Council agreed by a show of hands to pursue a tax ballot measure focused on city facilities and to advance the $400 million bond for future public hearings. Some members expressed concern about rising costs, the need for spending discipline, and the risk of failure at the ballot.
  • Vacancy excise tax ballot measure direction: Pollster Adam Probolsky reported that a vacancy tax on second and third homes had strong majority support, with about 70 percent more likely to vote yes after learning the details. Council members said the tax should target non-occupied second homes rather than rentals that are actively marketed. Council voted seven in favor to move the vacancy excise tax ballot measure forward for further consideration.
  • Fund Our Future community engagement results: Consultant Micah Intermill and budget analyst Stacy Polleycove presented results from Fund Our Future, which reached 599 residents through community conversations and an online survey. Wildfire response and prevention emerged as the strongest priority for renters and homeowners, with operational maintenance also widely supported. Renters strongly prioritized affordable housing while homeowners ranked it near the bottom, and the results will inform the 2027 budget and the long-term financial plan due in November.

entry.title: Boulder: June 18, 2026 - Boulder City Council Regular Meeting
entry.content:
The Council amended the agenda, heard extensive open comment on tipped worker wages, the Ponderosa mobile home park, Fort Chambers, Gaza, the Downtown Development Authority, and antisemitism, and approved the Juneteenth and Colorado Music Festival declarations and the consent agenda. It approved Resolution 1381 and an agreement with Spring Valley Mutual Water Association to annex Spring Valley Estates, then adopted Ordinance 8751 on special festival events and Ordinance 8752 on festival liquor permits with a $150 fee.

Most discussed: Development projects, Public comment, Equity & civil rights, Economic development, Labor & wages, Water & flooding

  • Call to order, roll call, and agenda amendment: The Mayor called the June 18, 2026 regular meeting to order and roll call confirmed a quorum. The Council voted 8-0 to add item 3B, a Colorado Music Festival 50th anniversary declaration, to the agenda.
  • Public comment on tipped worker wages and tip credit: Several labor organizers and workers spoke against increasing the tip credit or tip offset for restaurant workers. Speakers argued that a higher offset is a wage cut, that tipping is inequitable, and that restaurants already use service fees successfully. Staff later described outreach to about 100 restaurants and the Be Heard Boulder survey.
