  • Public comment on Ponderosa Mobile Home Park: Ponderosa residents spoke about the Habitat for Humanity and city redevelopment project and said the 2019 annexation promises to let residents stay in their homes are not being kept. They raised concerns about displacement, a road that would destroy homes, dark sky lighting, and traffic speed. Staff said they were unaware of the issues and committed to following up with residents.
  • Public comment on Fort Chambers interpretive design: A co-founder of Right Relationship Boulder objected to the Open Space and Mountain Parks interpretive design for Fort Chambers. She said the timeline starts with settlers, omits 13,000 years of Native presence, and removes a proposed reconstruction of the fort gates. Staff said it is meeting with Right Relationship and tribal partners.
  • Public comment on Gaza, Israel, and war investments: Speakers urged the Council to pass a resolution recognizing genocide in Gaza, divest from Israel, and stop investments tied to war. Other speakers criticized local defense jobs and called for stronger action on the city investment portfolio. Some speakers used inflammatory language that drew objections from the chair.
  • Public comment on the Downtown Development Authority: A resident speaking personally raised concerns about the proposed Downtown Development Authority tax increment financing. He estimated it could divert tens of millions of dollars from the library district and county, and he questioned voting by property owners who may not live in Boulder.
  • Public comment on Comprehensive Plan land use notification: A Gunbarrel resident said the city did not properly notify property owners about Boulder Valley Comprehensive Plan land use changes. She said notice was given only through utility bill inserts and online bills, and she estimated that mailed notices would cost about $41,000. She asked that the record reflect the notice deficiency.
  • Staff responses and council questions on open comment issues: Staff said the Fort Chambers project will involve further meetings and the DDA will return to Council on August 6. Staff explained how tip workers were notified through outreach, flyers, and surveys, and Council asked how the racial equity tool was used. Staff also clarified that Comprehensive Plan notice may be provided through utility bills without a physical letter.
  • Investment portfolio complaints: Councilmember Adams asked about the status of community complaints that the city investment portfolio includes oil and gas, tobacco, firearms, and private prison holdings. The city manager said he received a community communication, had not yet met with staff on it, and would share findings with Council. Staff also noted an internal review is underway.
  • Personal privilege on racism and antisemitism: A councilmember shared that she was subjected to a racial slur in public and that Black residents reported similar experiences. Council members condemned the harassment and discussed antisemitic harassment of a Jewish middle school student, a federal ADL complaint, and hate directed at Jewish residents in council chambers. Councilmembers called for public safety updates and more action on hate.
  • Recess and return to business: The Mayor called a recess at 6:22 p.m. to end open comment and resumed the business portion of the meeting later in the evening. The recess was procedural.
  • Juneteenth declaration: Councilmember Kaplan presented a declaration recognizing June 19, 2026 as Juneteenth in Boulder. The declaration describes the holiday's history, notes the city's flag raising since 2021 and holiday recognition since 2022, and pledges to oppose oppression. Dr. David Lewis Humphrey was present to receive the declaration.
  • Colorado Music Festival 50th anniversary declaration: Councilmember Marquis presented a declaration proclaiming July 9, 2026 as Colorado Music Festival Day in Boulder. The festival will hold its 50th season at Chautauqua Auditorium from July 9 through August 9 with more than 20,000 attendees. The festival representative thanked the Council and invited members to opening night.
  • Consent agenda approval: The Council approved consent agenda items 4A through 4D by a unanimous roll call vote. No questions or comments were raised on the consent items.
  • Call-up check-ins: Unity Church redevelopment and Mapleton demolition: The Council reviewed a concept plan to redevelop the Unity Church property at 2855 Folsom with 21 detached dwellings. A landmark alteration certificate to demolish an accessory building at 1039 Mapleton Avenue in the Mapleton Hill Historic District was also reviewed. No council member called either item up for further discussion.
  • Spring Valley Estates annexation staff presentation: Staff presented the proposed annexation of about 43 acres and 36 lots in Spring Valley Estates with initial zoning of Residential Estate. The annexation is by election, and Spring Valley Mutual Water Association would transition its water service to the city. Staff described terms including required public improvements, a local improvement district, plant investment fees, and a DOLA grant tied to a November 14 deadline.
  • Council questions on water rights, irrigation, and legal process: Council asked why the city is not acquiring the water association's water rights, and the Utilities Deputy Director said the quantity is low and not needed. Questions also covered agricultural water leases, irrigation use, and whether annexation terms restrict landscaping. Staff said annexation is legislative, that retroactive wildfire hardening requirements are legally risky, and that future costs would not fall on residents beyond the agreed terms.
  • Applicant presentation and wildfire risk: The attorney for Spring Valley Mutual Water Association presented the project, saying about 80 percent of residents supported moving forward. She emphasized wildfire risk from surrounding open space and the need for fire hydrants and adequate water pressure. The board member asked the city to waive the 90-day election blackout so the DOLA grant is not lost.
  • Public hearing on Spring Valley annexation: Speakers at the Spring Valley public hearing addressed the annexation resolution, though one speaker was ruled off topic and his time ended. Another resident urged the Council to base the cost allocation on buildable land rather than gross acreage and asked for market valuation of the pump house parcel. A former water board member criticized the proportional cost formula and asked for a cost per homeowner before voting.
  • Council discussion on election timing and cost allocation: The City Attorney explained that the municipal election code blackout of 90 days would require an ordinance or a state code approach that staff believes is unlikely to meet the grant timeline. Staff said the Planning Director expects only about four weeks gained from a special ordinance. Staff also explained that the cost allocation split 50 percent by lot area and 50 percent by house square footage and was recommended by the city consultant.
  • Votes adopting Resolution 1381 and water agreement: Councilmember Rob moved to adopt Resolution 1381 with findings and directing that an annexation election be called, and the Council approved it unanimously. The Council then unanimously authorized the city manager to execute the agreement with Spring Valley Mutual Water Association regarding annexation and transition of municipal services. The Mayor noted the decision will move the annexation toward an election.
  • Ordinance 8751 presentation on special festival events: Staff presented Ordinance 8751 to create a permitting process and standards for special festival events, such as the 2027 Sundance Film Festival. The ordinance adds definitions for events over 15,000 people, mobile food vehicle standards, and a comprehensive sign plan for temporary signs. Staff said the planning board unanimously recommended approval and that the ordinance would take effect 30 days after adoption.
  • Ordinance 8751 public comment and adoption: Council asked about undefined congestion standards, sign quality, minimum wage enforcement for vendors, and lessons learned from past events. A speaker opposed Sundance and the signs. The Council unanimously adopted Ordinance 8751 after a motion and second.
  • Ordinance 8752 festival liquor licenses and fees: Staff presented Ordinance 8752 to allow festival liquor licenses and permits and to set a $150 local fee to recover administrative review costs. Council debated whether the fee should be tied to revenue or cost recovery and whether fees should be audited. The Council unanimously adopted Ordinance 8752 after a motion and second.
  • Council employee evaluation timeline: Councilmember Spear shared the timeline for the 2026 council employee evaluation process. The survey launches July 7, closes July 28, and summaries are expected to be shared by late August. Merit increases would be retroactive to July 1.
  • Adjournment: The Mayor closed the meeting at 8:27 p.m. The adjournment was procedural.

entry.title: Boulder: June 11, 2026 City Council Study Session: 2026 State Legislative Update
entry.content:
Intergovernmental Affairs Officer Heather Staer reviewed the outcomes of the 2026 Colorado legislative session, including state budget cuts, bills the city supported or opposed, and the November 2026 ballot measures. Council asked questions on budget and grant impacts, wildfire and utility reliability, and data center bills, and gave feedback on future advocacy timing. Council reached consensus to direct staff to return with more information on the ballot measures, including Initiative 175, before taking formal positions by resolution at a future meeting.

Most discussed: Elections & ballot measures, Regional & state relations, Budget, Energy & utilities, Crime & justice, Council governance

  • Session Overview and Governor Action: The 2026 legislature met for a 120-day session from January 14 to May 13 and introduced about 626 bills, with roughly 450 sent to the governor. The governor had already vetoed 12 bills and had until the following day to act on the rest. The city took positions on 58 bills and posted a new bill tracker on its website.
  • State Budget Shortfall and Medicaid: The Joint Budget Committee had to cut about one billion dollars, leaving little room for new programs, and K-12 was prioritized. Medicaid costs are outpacing state revenue and drive much of the deficit. The legislature created a commission to recommend Medicaid policy changes by December, and a budget forecast is expected in June or July.
  • Federal Response, Immigration Bills, and Initiative 175 Counter-Measure: The majority party focused on responding to federal immigration policies, passing House Bill 1276 on civil liability for sharing immigration status information and detention center inspections. Election-year primaries highlighted tensions between moderate and progressive Democrats. House Bill 1430 was passed as a counter to Initiative 175, a road-funding initiative that could reduce local revenues, and proponents appear to be moving forward with the initiative.
  • City Priority Bills: Homelessness, AI, and Utility On-Bill Repayment: House Bill 1202 passed, allowing multi-jurisdictional homelessness authorities and requiring a state homelessness strategy. Senate Bill 189, which clarifies city responsibilities for automated decision-making and AI, passed and was signed. Senate Bill 148, the utility on-bill repayment program, failed in appropriations after a funding error and disputes over the unclaimed property trust fund, and staff will revisit it over the interim.
  • Direct and Indirect Budget Impacts on the City: The largest direct impact is the elimination of the local share of the retail marijuana sales tax, which will cost the general fund about 150,000 dollars. An amendment to preserve that share failed, though council can raise local marijuana taxes to close the gap. Multimodal transportation funding was cut by 10.5 million dollars, and affordable housing finance funding was reduced by about 130 million dollars statewide.
  • Dueling Data Center Bills: House Bill 1030 would have offered data center incentives without strong energy or environmental requirements, and the city opposed it. Senate Bill 102 would have set strict requirements for large-load data centers, and the city supported it. Both bills died in committee, and the Senate Bill 102 sponsors plan to bring a new version next session.
  • Housing and Land Use Legislation: The city supported Senate Bill 40, which expands the affordable homeownership program, and House Bill 1065, which creates transit and housing investment zones and a state tax credit for affordable housing. House Bill 1224 on mobile home park sales and resident fees also passed. The city opposed House Bill 1114 on minimum lot sizes and House Bill 1308 on lot splitting, and both failed in the Senate Local Government Committee.
  • Clean Energy Bills: The city supported several clean energy bills, including plug-in solar, which passed. House Bill 1226, addressing federal actions on coal plants, was also supported. The city helped defeat Senate Bill 208, which would have removed wind energy from Colorado's clean energy standards.
  • Firearm Safety Bills: The city opposed three bills that would have eroded local and state firearm safety laws, and all three were defeated. The city supported House Bill 1144, which adds guardrails around 3D printing of firearms, and it passed.
  • RTD Modernization (House Bill 1150): House Bill 1150 reduces the RTD board from 15 to nine members, with five elected and four appointed by the governor, and redraws district boundaries. The city sought seven elected seats, equity language in nominations, and a lower signature threshold, and only the signature threshold was restored to 250. The governor's office pointed to existing equity policies, so no additional equity language was added.
  • Looking Ahead: 2026 Election and 2027 Session Outlook: Democrats are expected to keep control of the legislature after the November 2026 general election, but a new governor and new House leadership may shift priorities. The state budget remains a problem, and a special session may be needed. Staff noted that August 3 is the deadline for initiative signatures and September 2 is when the final ballot will be known.
  • November Ballot Measures: Initiatives 85, 95, 108, 109, and 110: Staff described Initiative 85, which raises felony penalties for fentanyl and synthetic opioid offenses, mandates treatment for some drug felonies, and narrows exemptions. Initiative 95 requires law enforcement to notify federal immigration authorities in certain cases. Initiatives 108, 109, and 110 address child sex trafficking penalties, school athletics based on biological sex, and surgeries for minors.
  • Referred Measure SB 135 and Initiatives in Circulation: Senate Bill 135 refers a measure to voters to let the state keep revenue above the TABOR cap, up to 4.8 billion dollars, for K-12 and child programs. Initiative 175 would dedicate transportation taxes and fees to roads and bridges and could reduce general fund revenue by about 540 million dollars in future years. Initiatives 177 and 195, which would add a natural gas right and a graduated income tax, are still gathering signatures.
  • Council Questions on Budget Impacts and Grants: Council asked for an aggregate estimate of the city's exposure if the TABOR cap increase fails, and staff said a projection depends on state revenue forecasts and would come later in the budget process. Staff agreed to analyze Initiative 85 with the police chief, sheriff, and judge. Council also asked how Boulder's marijuana tax loss compares with other cities, and staff said the grant loss may affect Boulder more because it is a successful grant applicant.
  • Council Questions on Data Centers and Grants: Council asked how close the dueling data center bills came to passing and whether local home rule policies would be preempted. Staff said Senate Bill 102 preserved local control, and both bills stalled in committee because of labor and environmental opposition. Will Coin said data center incentives are losing bipartisan support.
  • Wildfire Risk and Utility Reliability: Council asked whether other communities share common goals on wildfire protection and power reliability that could support collective action. Staff said a utility civil immunity proposal was shut down last summer, and the Public Utilities Commission was reauthorized for seven years with quality-of-service plan requirements. A possible initiative, 308, could fund wildfire and forest work through a sporting goods sales tax.
  • Right to Natural Gas Initiative: A council member asked why the right to natural gas initiative was pursued, and staff said similar bills have failed for years in the legislature. Staff said the measure would preempt the city's building and energy conservation codes and remove local control over natural gas limits.
  • Advocacy Timing and Legislative Priorities: Council discussed when to start advocating for next year's legislation, and staff said outreach typically picks up in August and September. A council member proposed that council members send staff their ideas for legislation in July to build momentum before the fall priority-setting process. Staff noted that the election year may distract legislators.
  • Council Discussion of November Ballot Measures: Council members expressed concern about several measures, particularly Initiatives 108, 109, 110, and 95, which some said could harm transgender people or people seeking reproductive care. Others said Initiative 85 needs more analysis of its effects on sentencing and treatment. Council also noted that the group behind the measures is a dark money organization that spent heavily to gather signatures.
  • Next Steps for Ballot Position Decisions: Council agreed to ask staff for more information on all six ballot measures, including Initiative 175, before taking formal positions. Staff will return with research on who supports each measure and what each would affect, and it will consider positions by resolution at a future regular meeting. Council did not take a straw poll and moved on after reaching this direction.

entry.title: Boulder: June 4, 2026 - Boulder City Council and Planning Board Special Joint Meeting
entry.content:
The council and planning board held a joint public hearing on the recommended major update to the Boulder Valley Comprehensive Plan after a staff presentation on the plan's goals, policies, and future land use changes. Members questioned staff on the land use map, industrial and residential uses, housing goals, and notice to property owners, and the public spoke in large numbers, many raising concerns about density and notification. No final vote was taken; planning board will deliberate on June 16 and city council on June 25, 2026, and the council also approved its consent agenda, including a Pride Month proclamation.

Most discussed: Zoning, Public comment, Housing, Council governance, Affordable housing, Development projects

  • Pride Month Proclamation: The council presented a declaration recognizing June 2026 as Pride Month, commemorating the Stonewall events and recognizing local LGBTQ plus organizations. A representative of Rocky Mountain Equality accepted the proclamation and thanked the council for its support. The proclamation was part of the consent agenda items the council later approved.
  • Council Statements on Campus Group Letter and Hate Crime Sentencing: A council member used a point of personal privilege to condemn a University of Colorado student group's letter that defended the 2025 attack in Boulder. Another council member read a statement from the District Attorney about the life sentence and the commitment to fighting hate crimes. Both members asked colleagues to join in condemning the statement.
  • Consent Agenda Approval: The council approved consent agenda items 2A through 2F after a motion and second. The vote was unanimous on a roll call.
  • Staff Presentation on the Boulder Valley Comprehensive Plan Update: Staff presented the recommended major update, which followed about 20 months of engagement and included over a thousand comments on the March draft. The update sets 104 plain-language policies and a simplified future land use strategy with 12 designations, plus a new rural class and revised open space mapping. Staff explained that the plan sets direction over 20 years but does not guarantee specific outcomes, which will depend on future zoning and implementation. The presentation also outlined the four-body approval process and the schedule for county and city deliberations.
  • Questions on Land Use Map Changes, Maintenance Costs, and Wildfire Density: Council and board members asked for a delta map showing land use changes since the last draft, and staff agreed to prepare one for the June 16 meeting. A member asked for stronger plan language on funding long-term facility and infrastructure maintenance and on prioritizing affordable housing. Staff said the plan already elevates asset maintenance in policy 20 and funding stability in policy 64. Staff also confirmed that increasing density in neighborhood one near wildfire-prone areas would require zoning changes and evacuation review first.
  • Amendment Procedure and Timing: Staff explained that amendments must come from each body and must be specific, substantive changes rather than minor wording edits. Any change made by one body would require the other bodies to review it, possibly adding meetings into July, August, or September. The city attorney advised that planning board should submit suggestions through staff rather than through a chain of emails to avoid creating a public meeting outside the agenda.
  • Industrial Land and Residential Uses: Members asked whether residential uses are prohibited in industrial designations and whether the change would affect existing industrial tenants. Staff said residential is not described in the industrial classes but zoning still governs what is allowed, and that the revised plan aims to shift housing to other areas. Staff acknowledged that current use review does not offer strong protections for existing industrial tenants. Members said they would raise further questions at the June 16 meeting.
  • Affordable Housing Goal and Implementation Direction: A member questioned why the plan keeps a 15 percent affordable housing goal that may not be achievable by 2035. The housing director said the goal was intentionally aspirational and that the city should aim high. Staff said the citywide strategic plan and two-year council priority setting will provide implementation direction, and a suggestion was made to clarify the hierarchy of plans in the document.
  • Sub-Community Planning, Planning Reserve, and Groundwater: Members asked how sub-community and area planning guidance will be handled after being moved out of the plan into operational guidance. Staff said the existing process continues and that new sub-community plans will be developed and vetted with the boards. Staff also said the planning reserve process will be revisited through the intergovernmental agreement, which runs through 2042. Members also asked about groundwater protection, and staff said the state regulates groundwater and the city does not.
  • Public Hearing Testimony: Seventeen people signed up, each with two minutes, and speakers raised concerns about density, housing types, water supply, wildfire evacuation, and the survey design. The Boulder Chamber and a former planning board member urged restoring language allowing residential uses in industrial areas. Several speakers said residents were not properly notified about proposed land use changes and called for individual letters. Others supported the 15-minute neighborhood concept and asked for affordable housing requirements tied to upzoning.
  • Clarifying Questions on Notification and Survey Methods: Staff explained that property owners were notified through utility billing because mailing about 55,000 letters was impractical, and the city attorney said the notice complied with legal requirements. Staff said a national survey consultant reviewed and finalized the survey questions to make them statistically valid. Staff also clarified that outreach was open to all residents and was not specifically targeted at university students.
  • Motions to Continue the Hearing: The planning board voted seven to zero to continue the item to June 16, 2026, for deliberation and action. The council then unanimously voted to continue its deliberation and action on the plan to June 25, 2026. Both bodies noted that no additional public comment would be taken at those deliberation meetings, though emails would still be read.

entry.title: Boulder: May 28, 2026 - City of Boulder City Council Special Meeting and Study Session
entry.content:
Council unanimously endorsed Councilmember Matt Benjamin's nomination to the Colorado Municipal League Executive Board and unanimously approved Ordinance 8749 authorizing property acquisition, including eminent domain as a last resort, for the Arapahoe Avenue safety project. Council voted 5-3 to direct staff to research two airport land-use options and schedule a public hearing, then gave staff direction to draft DDA formation ballot measures for a November 2026 vote after discussing financial structure, parking transfers, and general fund impacts.

Most discussed: Economic development, Council governance, Budget, Legal & litigation, Taxes & fees, Transportation

  • Consent Agenda: CML Executive Board Nomination: Council added item 2A to the consent agenda to confirm its endorsement of Councilmember Matt Benjamin's nomination to the Colorado Municipal League Executive Board. Benjamin explained that Boulder holds two CML appointments and that the executive board sets CML's policy positions on state legislation. The consent agenda passed 8-0 with Benjamin recused.
  • Ordinance 8749: Arapahoe Avenue Right-of-Way Acquisition: Staff presented the East Arapahoe (CO 7) safety project, funded by a federal grant with $2.4 million in city match for a $12 million total, which requires temporary and permanent easements on 14 properties averaging about 700 square feet each. Staff said the eminent domain authority is needed to avoid schedule delays that could jeopardize the federal spending deadline in 2030, and that negotiation is expected to succeed. Council asked about property owner protections and budget placeholders, and one member of the public spoke in opposition. Council then unanimously approved Ordinance 8749.
  • Airport Land Use: Public Hearing and Research Direction: Staff presented scenario A, keeping the airport open indefinitely, and asked council whether to act by consent agenda or public hearing on a motion affirming continued airport use. Most council members favored a public hearing given community interest, and eight members raised hands for that option. Council then debated whether legal research on long-term land encumbrance and FAA grant implications should be done before a hearing, and five members voted to direct staff to bring back two options. Staff said the research would take time and that the budget process is a key pressure point.
  • DDA Formation: Plan of Development and Investment Priorities: Staff introduced a proposed Downtown Development Authority to reinvest in downtown and University Hill, citing flat downtown sales tax since 2020 and aging GID parking assets. The draft plan of development sets a 30-year framework with five priority areas: strategic site redevelopment, commercial corridor health, mixed-use development, public space investment, and connectivity. Staff stressed that the plan is a legal framework rather than a binding project commitment and that council approves the plan and budgets.
  • DDA Financial Structure: TIF, Mill Levy, and Parking Assets: The proposed financing combines tax increment financing, a 3.674 mill levy replacing existing GID levies, and parking asset integration. Staff projected about $1.8 million per year from the mill levy and roughly $18 to $26 million in cumulative six-year revenue across sources. Property tax TIF would capture about half of new growth within the boundary, while sales tax TIF captures growth above a 12-month baseline. Staff acknowledged that the financial impact on the general fund and other taxing entities still needs more analysis.
  • DDA Governance, Ballot Measures, and Timeline: Council would appoint the DDA board, approve the annual budget and plan amendments, and set terms of an intergovernmental agreement covering revenue sharing and parking asset transfers. Staff proposed three November 2026 ballot questions covering DDA formation, the mill levy, and TIF authorization, with a draft IGA returning August 6. Qualified electors include property owners, residents, and business lessees within the boundary, with an estimated 2,500 eligible electors. The timeline includes board formation and plan adoption around spring 2027 if approved.
  • Council Questions and Feedback on DDA Proposal: Council questioned how the DDA would affect general fund sales tax, school and library district property tax, parking rate authority, and measurement of economic outcomes. Members raised equity concerns that University Hill investment might be subordinated to downtown and asked for clearer accountability metrics and parking governance guardrails. Council members generally supported moving toward ballot measures while asking for more financial analysis before final decisions. Staff agreed to provide additional information on general fund impacts, parking asset sale proceeds, and draft IGA terms.
  • DDA Direction Vote and Study Session Close: Council provided direction on the draft plan, the financial structure, and staff drafting ballot measures for November 2026. Most members expressed support for moving forward, with some conditioning approval on more financial information. Staff confirmed they had enough direction to proceed and invited follow-up questions by email. The study session ended shortly after 8:30 p.m.

entry.title: Boulder: May 21, 2026 - Boulder City Council Regular Meeting (open comment, consent agenda, call-up check-ins, public hearing on Adjustment to Base Budget One, and matters from mayor and council on study sessions and straw polls)
entry.content:
Council heard extensive open comment on San Lazaro mobile home park residents seeking to buy their park, airport local control, Golden West senior housing utility changes, and minimum wage. It approved the consent agenda 8-0 except for Wallach's no vote on item 3B, and unanimously adopted Ordinance 8750 (Adjustment to Base Budget One, about $18.6 million). Council then discussed clarifying study session practice, straw poll terminology, and reconsideration rules, agreeing to use 'non-binding nod of five' language and to document informational study sessions in the rules of procedure.

Most discussed: Council governance, Elections & ballot measures, Legal & litigation, Affordable housing, Housing, Transportation

  • Open comment: San Lazaro mobile home park purchase: Multiple residents of San Lazaro mobile home park spoke about a notice of sale and risk of displacement, asking the city to help residents buy the park. A steering committee described a $42.5 million purchase price and concerns about private equity ownership. Staff said the city and county agreed to a new appraisal, that financial support options are being explored, and that the city supports the effort.
  • Open comment: airport local control and ballot measure: Several speakers urged council to maintain local control of the municipal airport and avoid FAA grant obligations, citing noise, leaded fuel, and aviation safety. Others argued the airport is a science and disaster-response resource. Speakers asked for a ballot measure and a do-over on study session information. Staff responded that funding decisions and CDOT funding limits are under review and the airport will return to council soon.
  • Open comment: Golden West senior housing utilities and parking: Golden West residents, many seniors on fixed incomes, said the Boulder Housing Partners lease change ending bundled cable, TV and telephone service would cost them, and raised parking fees and elevator problems. Staff said the Comcast contract expired, free Wi-Fi continues, and rents drop about $40 to $45 per month, but additional services cost more. Council asked BHP for follow-up information and support options.
  • Open comment: minimum wage and vacancy tax: A resident opposed a proposed refusal to raise the tipped minimum wage in line with a 2024 study, arguing that wage freezes reduce buying power and drive workers away. He proposed a Boulder vacancy tax to address rising rents instead. Another speaker asked the city to speed up development review for trees and energy-efficient homes. Council received these comments as part of open comment.
  • Consent agenda approval (items 3A and 3B): Council approved the consent agenda, which included items 3A and 3B, by voice roll call. Councilmember Wallach voted no on item 3B, an ordinance amending Title 7 height limitations, citing sloppy drafting. The motion passed with that one exception.
  • Call-up check-ins: 777 Broadway site review and 990 Arapahoe landmark: Council reviewed call-up items for a site review at 777 Broadway for 63 residential units and a Landmarks Board decision not to designate 990 Arapahoe Avenue. No one called up either item. Councilmember Matt then commented on the landmarking process, suggesting reform at next year's retreat because of its effect on senior affordable housing and displacement.
  • Public hearing: Ordinance 8750, Adjustment to Base Budget One: Staff presented the first 2026 adjustment to base totaling about $18.6 million, including $13.1 million from fund balance, $5.3 million from mid-year grants, and $129,000 from additional revenue. Items included business incentives, wildfire programs, affordable housing carryover, and a $7.3 million radio replacement purchased early at a discount. Council questioned fund balance levels and communications staffing, and the ordinance was adopted unanimously after a public hearing with no speakers in favor or against.
  • Matters from mayor and council: study sessions, straw polls, and reconsideration: City Attorney Teresa Tate explained that study sessions give non-binding direction to staff, that straw polls are not addressed in procedure, and that reconsideration applies only after a material change in law or fact, requiring five votes to schedule. Council discussed the confusion from a recent study session on the airport and agreed to use 'non-binding nod of five' language. Council also agreed to document informational study sessions in the rules of procedure and to review CAC agenda item titles.

entry.title: Boulder: May 14, 2026 - City of Boulder City Council Study Session
entry.content:
Council received a financial forecast from CU's Business Research Division and city staff showing flattening sales and property tax revenue, a projected $6.5 million general fund shortfall for 2027, and 4% department reduction targets. Council then reviewed potential 2026 ballot measures and facility funding scenarios and gave staff direction to poll on a parks and public improvement mill levy expansion, up to $200 million in debt (with a split test at $400 million), a charter change to the debt limit, and a general fund debt authorization, while not pursuing a vacancy tax further at this time.

Most discussed: Budget, Elections & ballot measures, Taxes & fees, Council governance, Economic development, Parks & recreation

  • Economic conditions and sales tax outlook: CU's Business Research Division reviewed national and Colorado economic conditions, noting slow GDP growth, stalled job growth, and a sharp rise in energy prices and inflation. Retail spending remains nominally positive but declines after adjusting for inflation, and Boulder's sales tax growth trails the state average. Staff's forecast uses the Moody's national outlook and a medium scenario, projecting slow but steady sales and use tax growth.
  • Council questions on economy, recession risk, and water: Council members asked how long energy price effects would last, whether conditions signal recession, and why Colorado is losing jobs. Questions also covered the Federal Reserve, tariffs, and property versus sales tax ratios. A council member noted that water supply was not a variable in the forecast model, and staff said alternative scenarios would address unanticipated shocks.
  • City financial forecast and 2027 budget outlook: Staff reported that the 2026 budget closed a $7.5 million gap through hiring freezes, realignments, and a 7.8% general fund reduction. For 2027, a $6.5 million general fund shortfall led to a request for 4% department reductions. Sales and use tax and property tax revenues are revised down, with the property tax reassessment showing only 0.2% actual value growth.
  • Forecast Q&A, performance-based cuts, and Sundance revenue: Council asked whether programs were cut based on performance measures and how staff would communicate reductions to the public. Members questioned why the medium forecast scenario was chosen and requested more programmatic budget-to-actual detail. Staff said Sundance revenue will be included in the sales tax model as it is received, with a cautious approach in year one.
  • Long-term financial strategy and ballot measure framing: The city manager explained that about 68% of city revenue is committed to specific purposes, so the general fund is constrained. Expense growth has outpaced revenue growth, and a long-term comprehensive financial plan is planned for late 2026. Staff framed the ballot measure work as one component of that strategy.
  • Staff ballot measure options and recommendations: Staff presented four tax ballot options for further exploration: a parks and public improvement mill levy or use expansion, a residential vacancy excise tax, general fund debt authorization, and a public realm sales tax consolidation. Staff recommended polling the parks mill levy and deferring the general fund debt, public realm tax, and vacancy tax to later analysis. Polling is limited to three to four items, with results expected in late June.
  • Facility funding scenarios for priority buildings: Staff reported that 15 priority buildings need roughly $20 million over five to six years for major maintenance, with an estimated $500 million total priority need. Scenarios A through E combined existing CCRS authority with mill levy increases and general obligation bonds. Staff recommended scenarios C and E, which together provide up to $200 million, and a charter change to the 3% debt limit based on actual value.
  • Council direction on polling and ballot items: Council members debated how many items to poll and whether to include the $400 million option, with several supporting a $200 million split test. Many supported polling general fund debt authorization because it could inform future planning, while others raised concerns about taxpayer fatigue. Council also discussed whether the mill levy expansion should include operations, public safety, and the airport.
  • Vacancy excise tax direction: Council members discussed a residential vacancy excise tax on homes vacant at least 183 days, with some proposing a tiered structure based on square footage and a higher maximum. Staff said the legal details would require further research, and council gave consensus to proceed with that analysis. Some members favored an ordinance over a ballot initiative for greater future flexibility, and others raised concerns about unintended consequences.
  • Charter amendments on boards and wildfire mitigation: The charter committee proposed revising charter section 130 on boards and commissions, which failed by 65 votes in 2024, and adding wildfire mitigation as an explicit open space purpose in section 176. Council members debated timing, removal provisions, and whether to add flood mitigation. Staff said wildfire work is already permitted, and council gave direction to continue drafting the wildfire language but not advance the boards and commissions change this year.
  • Community petitions and state and regional ballot measures: Staff noted one community-sponsored petition for a commercial and residential vacancy tax, included in the council packet. Boulder County, the city of Boulder, and Boulder Valley School District ballot measures remain to be determined. Staff also provided information on state ballot measures and said a legislative update would come in June.
  • Adjournment: A council member requested a future agenda item to take positions on several ballot measures. The mayor then closed the study session at 9:23 p.m.

entry.title: Boulder: May 7, 2026 - City of Boulder City Council Regular Meeting
entry.content:
The May 7, 2026 Boulder City Council regular meeting opened with extended public comment on proposed tipped minimum wage changes, a residential vacancy tax, and FAA airport grants, and included a Missing and Murdered Indigenous Persons declaration. Council approved the consent agenda, unanimously adopted Ordinance 8741 to landmark 745 University Avenue as the Polls and Registration House, and reviewed call-up items including the Presbyterian Manor concept plan. Council adopted Ordinance 8745, the Omnibus land use code amendment, on second reading by a 5 to 1 vote, with an added amendment removing outdoor patio size limits for breweries and related venues.

Most discussed: Zoning, Public comment, Parking, Historic preservation, Labor & wages, Economic development

  • Call to Order, Roll Call and Removal of Item 4E: Mayor Brockett called the meeting to order and the council confirmed a quorum. Council unanimously voted to remove item 4E from the consent agenda, which kept the June 11 study session as scheduled rather than canceling it for an in-person special meeting.
  • Open Comment Period: Residents spoke for two minutes each, with many opposing cuts to the tipped minimum wage and citing the city's living wage figures. Speakers urged the council to place a residential vacancy tax on the ballot at $5,000 per unit, opposed FAA grants that would commit the airport in perpetuity, and raised concerns about land use rules affecting a lot split. Other speakers addressed South Boulder Rec Center pool closure concerns, a Bike Boulder bike registration drive, and the Israel and Gaza divestment issue. Staff said a tip credit discussion will return later in the year, and council said a July public hearing on tip offsets was planned. Council members used their closing remarks to thank speakers and respond to comments.
  • National Day of Awareness for Missing and Murdered Indigenous Persons Declaration: Council Member Adams presented a declaration recognizing the National Day of Awareness for Missing and Murdered Indigenous Persons, and the mayor signed it. The declaration calls on city departments to recognize root causes and calls on Boulder law enforcement to receive Colorado-specific training. Speakers from Harvest of All First Nations and community connectors asked for real action beyond proclamations, including reparations, land access, and accountability. A speaker also warned that surveillance tools like license plate readers could increase criminalization of Indigenous communities. Council thanked the speakers and committed to continued efforts to keep residents safe and heard.
  • Consent Agenda: Council considered the consent agenda, which included items 4A through 4D and 4F through 4L, with item 4E previously removed. A council member asked about the beverage licensing authority rules amendment, and staff confirmed a public hearing would occur on second reading. Council then approved the consent agenda unanimously by roll call.
  • Call-Up Check-Ins and Presbyterian Manor Concept Plan: Council reviewed call-up items 5A through 5F, including landmark alteration applications for 409 Mountain View Road and relocation of two buildings at 2106 Arapahoe Avenue. Item 5D was a height modification at 1039 Mapleton Avenue, and item 5E was an outside city utility permit at 1420 Cherryvale Road. For item 5F, the concept plan for permanently affordable senior housing at Presbyterian Manor, staff explained that potential code changes on demolition timing would not apply to this application. Council members raised questions on timing and tax credits, but no items were called up for further review.
  • Landmark Designation of 745 University Avenue (Ordinance 8741): Staff presented a request to designate the 1907 house at 745 University Avenue as an individual landmark, to be named the Polls and Registration House. The house served as a polling place for two decades, hosted caucuses and World War I registration, and was the site of 1917 municipal elections that created the city charter and proportional voting. The owners, Celeste Landry and Eric Cornell, spoke about the house's voting history, and Historic Boulder supported the designation. Council unanimously adopted Ordinance 8741 by roll call, making it the city's 222nd individual landmark.
  • Omnibus Land Use Code Amendment (Ordinance 8745): Staff presented the Omnibus code amendment, a cleanup ordinance that removes office floor area limits, clarifies ADU utilities, allows driveways to remain after garage conversions, and allows height modifications up to 55 feet for three-story community, cultural, or educational uses. Council added an amendment removing outdoor patio size limits for breweries, tap rooms, and tasting rooms, which the staff confirmed could return on third reading. Council members raised concerns about the height change and the breadth of eligible uses, and asked staff to narrow the list. Council voted 5 to 1 to amend and pass Ordinance 8745 on second reading, with third reading expected at the next business meeting.

entry.title: Boulder: April 23, 2026 - City of Boulder City Council Study Session
entry.content:
The study session covered two items: the future of Boulder Municipal Airport, including whether to operate it indefinitely (scenario one) or keep the closure option open by forgoing FAA grants (scenario two), and an update on power resilience and public safety power shutoffs with a proposed roadmap and engagement plan. On the airport, a straw poll showed five members favoring scenario one and four favoring scenario two, and council directed staff to bring back formal action at a future meeting. On power resilience, council expressed alignment with the proposed analysis, policy options, and engagement approach, with the community council forum planned for October.

Most discussed: Public health, Council governance, Budget, Public comment, Flock cameras, Elections & ballot measures

  • Boulder Municipal Airport Future Operations: Staff presented updated financial projections showing scenario one (indefinite operation with FAA grants) would require no added local subsidy, while scenario two (forgoing grants until 2040) would require about $600,000 per year in other local funds. Staff noted the FAA considers the city already bound to operate the airport in perpetuity and that the city's lawsuit was dismissed on jurisdictional grounds. Council members debated the financial risk, fiduciary responsibility, perpetuity covenants, noise, lead fuel, and the appropriateness of deciding via study session. A straw poll favored scenario one 5 to 4, and council asked staff to return with formal action.
  • Airport Community Conversation and Regulatory Authority: Staff reviewed the 2023 airport community conversation, which heard mixed views with no clear consensus, and explained that aviation noise and leaded fuel are federally regulated, so the city cannot ban leaded fuel or directly regulate aircraft noise. Staff described noise mitigation steps and a plan to transition to unleaded fuel by 2030 pending FAA approval. Council discussed how these limits affect community health and noise concerns.
  • Airport Financial Outlook and Land Reuse: Staff updated 14-year financial projections and noted pavement reconstruction costs of roughly $16 million could arise under scenario two. Staff also presented a preliminary broker opinion of value of about $1 million per acre and remediation estimates of $10 to 30 million for potential future redevelopment. Council members questioned the figures and the potential for land sales or affordable housing use.
  • Airport Legal Status and Perpetuity Covenants: Council discussed whether accepting new FAA grants would create perpetual covenants and whether council should weigh in on grant conditions, which staff said is largely operational. Staff said the city can request decommissioning at any time, though the FAA has indicated the city is already encumbered in perpetuity. Council members questioned whether a perpetual commitment would be appropriate without a broader policy.
  • Council Straw Poll and Process for Formal Action: After public comment-style remarks from members, a straw poll showed five members favoring scenario one and four favoring scenario two. Council members objected to making a consequential decision at a study session and asked for formal action at a future regular meeting. Staff said council may act by motion or resolution and that the existing ordinance already provides for an airport, so formal reaffirmation is optional but possible.
  • Power Resilience and Public Safety Power Shutoffs: Staff presented the growing frequency and duration of outages from Xcel Energy public safety power shutoffs, aging underground equipment, and weather damage. Staff described Xcel's wildfire mitigation strategies, including undergrounding about 5.5 miles of line north of Boulder and sectionalizing foothill lines. Council was asked to confirm the proposed analysis, roadmap, and engagement approach, and members gave thumbs-up support.
  • Community Engagement and Power Resilience Roadmap: Staff outlined a phased engagement plan with summer strategic outreach to frontline, business, and medical-needs communities and a fall community and council forum, with a roadmap due by year end. Council members discussed accountability for Xcel's commitments, metrics for tracking reliability, coordination with existing reporting requirements, and the need for financial information before the budget cycle. Council supported the approach and asked for cross-departmental tradeoff analysis.

entry.title: Boulder: April 16, 2026 - Regular City Council Meeting (Thursday evening session)
entry.content:
Council heard extended public comment on the South Boulder Rec Center, the Boulder Airport, Flock and AI surveillance, tipped wage credits, bear trash rules, and the Fund Our Future survey. It approved the consent agenda unanimously, and adopted Ordinance 8748 unanimously on second reading to create a local framework for commercial metropolitan districts, with the companion model service plan resolution deferred to the next regular meeting for a compounding-interest change. Council also received a state legislative update and set its positions on several bills.

Most discussed: Development projects, Economic development, Transportation, Open space, Parks & recreation, Public comment

  • Open Public Comment Period: Residents signed up to speak in person and online on a wide range of topics. Speakers addressed the transportation maintenance fee and religious facilities, the Boulder Airport, the South Boulder Rec Center, Flock and AI surveillance, tipped wage credits, bear trash carts, and retaliation concerns. Staff and council responded briefly, with council reminding speakers not to criticize individual staff members by name.
  • South Boulder Rec Center and Fund Our Future Survey: Many residents urged council to keep a pool, gym, and core amenities at the South Boulder Rec Center rather than funding a new facility. Speakers said the Fund Our Future questionnaire does not give a clear option to preserve South Boulder's core services and that indoor aquatic programming maps to East and North expansions. Staff said the survey is a prioritization exercise with a notes section and encouraged participation. Council members asked staff to clarify Scenario A (new building, no pool) versus Scenario B (pool and gym at current service levels).
  • Boulder Airport Future: Speakers described the airport as a wildfire aviation base, medevac hub, science research site, and economic engine, and asked council to keep it open. Speakers also cited EAA youth flight programs, pilot training, and recent unleaded fuel availability. One business owner urged council to return to accepting FAA grants and avoid further delay. Council did not take action on the airport during this meeting.
  • Flock and AI Surveillance Concerns: A speaker urged council to ban AI-enabled surveillance, arguing that Flock and similar live-view camera systems upload footage to outside servers and erode privacy. The speaker said switching Denver to a less harmful vendor was only a partial fix. No council action was taken on this item.
  • Tipped Wage Credit Proposal: Several speakers opposed any increase to the tipped wage credit, arguing it would reduce workers' pay and consumer confidence. Council members said they were hearing from both restaurant owners and workers and wanted more data on affected groups. The conversation remained public comment and did not result in a vote.
  • Bear Protection Trash Ordinance Review: The Boulder Bear Coalition presented a paper on the 2014 bear-resistant trash ordinance, which led to roughly 14,700 carts by 2016. The group asked the city to review the ordinance, which has not had a comprehensive review since about 2018, and to share lessons learned. Staff said they have received the proposal and are reviewing it, and that any new ordinance would require council direction.
  • Transportation Maintenance Fee Exemptions for Places of Worship: A faith community leader asked council to exempt worshipping communities from the transportation maintenance fee, noting that BVSD and CU are exempt under state law. She also asked council to audit zoning that conflicts with the comprehensive plan and to reconsider landmark review for older religious buildings. Council asked staff about the timeline for exemptions, and staff said they would follow up.
  • Consent Agenda: Council approved consent agenda items 3A through 3I unanimously. Item G related to the Spring Valley Estates annexation, and staff confirmed that water lines have not yet been installed and residents would pay for that infrastructure. Council also discussed Ordinance 8745 on land use code cleanup, including three-story educational and cultural facilities, and a request to address brewery retail square footage limits.
  • Metropolitan Districts Ordinance and Model Service Plan: Staff presented Ordinance 8748 and Resolution 1378 to create a local review process for commercial metropolitan districts, including a 90% commercial threshold, a 50-mill debt cap, a 65-mill aggregate cap, and a 40-year debt limit. Public comment raised concerns about property tax burdens and displacement, and council questioned staff on compounding interest, mill levy caps, and the policy alternatives. Council straw-polled a change to allow compounding interest for developer debt if an external advisor certifies it, and Ordinance 8748 was then adopted unanimously while the resolution was deferred to the next regular meeting.
  • Legislative Update from the State: Heather Staer reviewed the 2026 General Assembly session, which ends May 13, and a roughly $1.2 billion budget deficit driving cuts. Priority bills included HB 1202 on regional homelessness response, SB 148 on-bill repayment for energy upgrades, and an AI policy bill still awaiting introduction. Staff also reviewed HB 1308 on lot splitting, where council agreed to an oppose-unless-amended position, and SB 150 on RTD reform, where council asked for seven elected board members and a lower signature threshold. Council set its positions on the bills.

entry.title: Boulder: April 9, 2026 City of Boulder City Council Study Session
entry.content:
The study session covered two items: the Boulder Arts Blueprint, a 10-year arts and culture roadmap with seven goals, and the facilities investment strategy, including a $20 million minimum repair need across 15 priority buildings and recreation center scenarios. Council gave staff feedback rather than making decisions, and expressed general support for staff's recommendations to fund minimum infrastructure needs first with available funds and to develop investment scenarios for May. Council asked for clearer data, outcome-based metrics, and more information on funding levers and costs before choosing among options.

Most discussed: Budget, Arts, culture & libraries, Council governance, Parks & recreation, Fire & EMS, Development projects

  • Boulder Arts Blueprint Overview and Council Questions: Arts and culture staff presented the Boulder Arts Blueprint, a 10-year roadmap aligned with the Comprehensive Plan and built on roughly 2,000 community engagements. The plan has seven goals covering accessibility, workforce, public art, nonprofits, and experimentation, and is funded largely through the Arts, Culture, and Heritage Tax and the 1% for Art policy. Council members asked about staffing capacity, funding during sales tax downturns, Sundance Festival impacts, and the lack of baseline KPI data. Staff said grant funding rose to $2 million and that an arts fund would seek independent money.
  • Council Feedback on the Arts Blueprint Implementation Approach: Council members expressed support for the arts approach but raised concerns about the number of goals, unclear prioritization, and missing metrics, reporting frequency, and baselines. Several cited staff capacity limits and recent wildfires as reasons to focus on priorities. The Mayor praised the work and deferred prioritization to staff. Council member comments also called for supporting artists' affordability, intellectual property protection, and climate-linked venue improvements.
  • Facilities Investment Strategy Overview and Building Portfolio Condition: Staff described the history of the city's 75-plus buildings, roughly 2 million square feet with an average age near 50 years, and the creation of the Facilities and Fleet department in 2020. The 2021 facilities plan found the portfolio declining faster than reinvestment, and consolidation to the Western City campus is expected to remove more than $20 million in unfunded liability. Staff grouped buildings into categories and identified 15 priority buildings with about $20 million in minimum repair needs and roughly $500 million in full modernization costs, of which $400 million is unfunded.
  • Recreation Center Scenarios and Staff Recommendations: Parks and Recreation staff presented condition reports for the South Boulder, East Boulder, and North Boulder recreation centers, with East needing urgent repairs and a first phase planned for 2027 construction. Two scenarios were outlined for each center, with Scenario A sustaining service levels and Scenario B adding amenities, and the Parks and Recreation Advisory Board preferred Scenario B for all three centers. Staff recommended funding minimum infrastructure needs first with existing CCRS funds, about $2 million a year, and developing investment scenarios for May 14. Council discussed pool costs, electrification, and renovation versus new build.
  • Council Questions on Costs, Codes, Consolidation, and Property Disposal: Council asked how to weigh sustainability goals against cost, whether code requirements drive costs, and whether fire stations or police facilities could consolidate. Staff said international building codes drive much of the cost, and a fire station analysis supported the Station 4 location near CU South. Questions also covered disposing of surplus property such as the land at the current public safety site, seeking CU financial partnership, and why the unfunded liability grew from $380 million to $400 million. Staff said the $400 million reflects new buildings meeting modern codes rather than repairs.
  • Reserves, Civic Area Project, and Value Engineering: Council asked whether reserves could fund urgent projects, and the budget officer said the reserve policy targets emergencies and natural disasters rather than capital projects. Council also asked whether the Civic Area project should be deferred, and staff explained it was advanced for park condition, economic vitality, and the East Bookend opportunity. Council members asked whether project costs could be value-engineered, and staff said current estimates use industry standards and that a 100,000-square-foot public safety building would exceed $100 million.
  • Council Straw Poll on Staff Recommendations: Council discussed whether staff's first recommendation to fund minimum infrastructure needs with current funds should proceed. Several members asked for more data on debt service, disposal proceeds, and lease savings before deciding on the broader strategy. Council members ultimately said yes to funding minimum infrastructure needs, and Council members agreed to develop investment scenarios across priority buildings, with results to inform the ballot measure, the 2027 budget, and the six-year CIP.
  • Council Priorities and Closing Remarks: Council members gave direction on priorities including a sequence for recreation center projects, transparent disposal and lease policies, and a facilities advisory structure modeled on school district committees. Members asked for scenarios that show equity, climate, and framework alignment as well as community-preference criteria, and urged early cost clarity for residents. Several members asked that rec center services not decline and that staff seek budget savings. The Mayor thanked staff and the community, and the study session closed with remarks from the city manager and Council.

entry.title: Boulder: April 2, 2026 Boulder City Council Regular Meeting (Thursday evening session)
entry.content:
The council heard extensive open comment on the South Boulder Rec Center future, tipped wage credit, and open space, then approved a consent agenda (with Council Member Adams voting no on item 4E related to Area III) and adopted Ordinance 8743 on a unanimous 8-0 vote expanding festival lodging rental licenses to tenants with owner consent for Sundance. The council also began exploring local authority to modify the tip offset, straw-polling to remove option three and keep the status quo, 2A, 2B, and a Benjamin sunset proposal, with staff directed to return with timing details through CAC.

Most discussed: Labor & wages, Economic development, Taxes & fees, Housing, Public comment, Parks & recreation

  • Open Comment: South Boulder Rec Center and Pool: Many residents, including children and seniors, spoke in favor of preserving the South Boulder Rec Center pool, gym, and walkability for families. Speakers questioned the lack of a repair or cost analysis and the option of saving the existing building, while others urged prioritizing South Boulder in capital investment. Staff acknowledged the passion and said holistic facility data would come to council the following week.
  • Open Comment: Tipped Wage Credit: Speakers including labor organizers, tipped workers, restaurant owners, and a clinic employee debated a proposed freeze or increase in the tip credit. Labor advocates warned of income losses and wage theft, while restaurant voices cited slow sales and rising costs. Several speakers suggested a vacancy tax or other business support instead.
  • Open Comment: Open Space Sales Tax Ballot Measure: A resident whose in-laws campaigned for the 1967 open space sales tax urged council not to advance a ballot measure that would change the dedicated open space tax. She emphasized protecting public lands permanently.
  • Arts Week Declaration: Council Member Benjamin presented a declaration for Boulder Arts Week, April 3 through April 12, 2026, highlighting the creative sector's economic impact and the new Boulder Arts Blueprint. Dr. Nicholas Felder, the 2026 Bright Futures Award recipient, accepted the declaration and spoke about art's role in community.
  • Consent Agenda: Council approved items 4A through 4Q on the consent agenda, including a 10-year water lease with the Town of Erie, which staff said would not jeopardize local supply during drought watch. Council Member Adams voted no on the Area III service expansion framework item. Staff committed to follow up on timing of the battery storage sales tax change.
  • Call-Up Check-Ins: Council reviewed items 5A through 5D, including a synagogue site review amendment, a water tap request in Area III, a student housing site review at 28th Street and College Avenue, and a landmark alteration in Mapleton Hill. A motion to call up the student housing project for Design Advisory Board referral was withdrawn after staff said DAB had already reviewed it unanimously.
  • Public Hearing: Festival Lodging Rental Ordinance 8743: Staff presented an ordinance creating a festival lodging license tier for properties with long-term rental licenses, with a one-year term and $75 fee, allowing tenants to participate with owner consent. Speakers included a resident opposed to Sundance-related growth, Barha representing landlords who requested a vacant-units-only option, and a housing official who supported the ordinance as written. Council discussed revenue split transparency, tenant protections, and application timing before adopting the ordinance 8-0.
  • Tip Offset Exploration and Straw Polls: Staff presented options for modifying the tip offset under newly granted local authority, ranging from status quo to a maximized offset that would cut tipped base wages. Council Member Benjamin proposed freezing the tipped base wage at $13.80 with a January 2029 sunset. In straw polls, option three was removed, while status quo, 2A, 2B, and the Benjamin proposal stayed on the table. Council directed staff to return on timing and data availability through CAC, with a June 18 hearing under reconsideration.

entry.title: Boulder: March 26, 2026 - Boulder City Council Study Session (joint with Planning Board)
entry.content:
Boulder Valley School District presented declining enrollment, with about 3,600 fewer students since 2017 and a projected further drop of about 1,700, and outlined community engagement sessions in April with possible school consolidation decisions in fall 2026. Council then met with the Planning Board to review the draft Boulder Valley Comprehensive Plan, with consensus on strong support for housing diversity, 15-minute neighborhoods, and the simplified land use framework, while a straw poll on expanding neighborhood-two designations along transit corridors did not reach consensus. No formal votes were taken; refinements return at the April 13 four-body meeting, with public comments due April 6 and adoption hearings planned for June.

Most discussed: Zoning, Housing, Regional & state relations, Wildfire, Council governance, Transportation

  • BVSD Declining Enrollment Update: Boulder Valley School District leaders presented enrollment data showing a sustained decline of more than 3,600 students since 2017, with about 525 lost this year alone and a projected further drop of about 1,700 students. Elementary schools are most affected, with roughly 4,800 open seats district-wide and many Boulder schools falling below two classes per grade level. The district outlined community engagement sessions in April, staff option development over the summer, and a final plan for board action in October, with potential consolidations or closures and a stated goal of reinvesting savings in classrooms. Council members asked about long-term projections, the city role in reusing surplus buildings, and how the city can get involved early in neighborhood-level changes.
  • Comprehensive Plan Overview by Staff: Staff presented the draft Boulder Valley Comprehensive Plan, reorganized into six chapters with a new implementation chapter and glossary, and reduced the policy list from 210 to 102. The update was shaped by 69 engagement opportunities, community assembly recommendations, and 23 community change requests moved into the draft. The draft simplifies the future land use map into four classes and 12 designations, shifting from parcel-by-parcel mapping to neighborhood-scale planning. Staff projected about a 35 percent increase in housing capacity, more balanced housing types, and about 11 percent more job capacity, while noting these are modeled estimates rather than forecasts.
  • Council Clarifying Questions on the Draft Plan: Council asked why some policies, such as those on the municipal airport and specific financing tools, are more operational than others, and staff said the goal is to keep the plan visionary with examples rather than fixed rules. Questions covered how the plan addresses wildfire fuels mitigation, whether zoning will conflict with new land use designations, and how the strategic plan and department plans will be approved, with the answer that council will vote on the citywide strategic plan. Members also asked about student versus non-student population growth, community hub capacity, the mismatch between transportation and land use, and how the plan connects to the 2023 community survey.
  • Consensus on Alignment and Strongly Supported Elements: Members broadly agreed the draft reflects community feedback, praising the depth of engagement and the community assembly contributions. Strong support was expressed for the expanded housing types in neighborhood one and two areas, the 15-minute neighborhood concept, the integration of land use and transportation, and new policies on social infrastructure, natural infrastructure, and the night and visitor economy. Several members also praised the equity-focused first policy and the simplified land use designations, while one member stressed the need for stronger acknowledgment of tribal treaties and land back.
  • Refinements, Neighborhood Character, and Transit Corridor Designations: Members suggested refinements including clearer transportation and Vision Zero language, stronger wildfire and fuels mitigation in open space policies, better emergency communication language, clearer service level agreement processes for water, and a glossary definition for neighborhood character. Discussion of policy 24 on neighborhood character was contentious, with some arguing the term is exclusionary and others defending it as describing neighborhood personality. Planning Board members and council split on a straw poll to have staff study expanding neighborhood-two designations beyond transit corridors, with no consensus reached. Staff agreed to report back with proposed revisions and flagged items needing city-county discussion on April 13.
  • Next Steps and Adoption Timeline: Staff asked members to send written feedback to the project email by April 6, the close of the public comment period, and noted that all comments will be logged with rationale and shared with the recommended plan. A four-body meeting with the county commissioners and planning commission is set for April 13 to resolve lingering issues. The recommended plan will be released May 18, with a joint public hearing on June 4. Staff confirmed that the plan becomes effective upon final approval by all four bodies.

entry.title: Boulder: March 12, 2026 - City of Boulder City Council Study Session
entry.content:
The council held a study session covering a Boulder Strong Day of Remembrance declaration, a preliminary look at forming a Downtown Development Authority (DDA) with tax increment financing and a possible November 2026 ballot, and a preliminary discussion of potential 2026 tax ballot measures. Council supported continued refinement of the DDA model with standalone governance and fiscal safeguards, and in the ballot discussion narrowed options to moving forward with the mid-range public realm mill levy, residential vacancy excise tax, general fund debt authorization, and combining dedicated sales taxes, while dropping the transformational and other mid-range options for 2026.

Most discussed: Budget, Development projects, Elections & ballot measures, Taxes & fees, Council governance, Economic development

  • Boulder Strong Day of Remembrance Declaration: Councilmember Wallach presented a declaration designating March 22 as the Boulder Day of Remembrance to honor the ten people killed in the 2021 King Soopers mass shooting. He read the victims' names and announced a remembrance ceremony at the Boulder Museum on March 22. The declaration was introduced as a ceremonial item before the work sessions began.
  • Downtown Development Authority Formation and Analysis: Staff presented the proposed DDA as a tool to capture tax increment from property and sales tax growth within a study area and reinvest in downtown and the Hill. Staff's initial direction was a standalone DDA with a 1-2 year transition, a plan of development, and possible transfer of parking assets, with a June return to council and a possible November ballot. Council asked clarifying questions about voting thresholds, liability, base year, revenue sharing, and staff capacity. Most members supported continued refinement of the model, while Taisha Adams urged that climate and nature be included in the analysis.
  • Preliminary Discussion of 2026 Tax Ballot Measures: Finance staff presented the long-term financial strategy, noting that 68% of city revenue is dedicated and sales tax is flattening. Staff reviewed transformational, mid-range, and structural ballot measure options and the timeline toward a May 14 narrowing and a June polling result. Council straw polls kept the mid-range public realm mill levy, residential vacancy excise tax, general fund debt authorization, and combining dedicated sales taxes for further work, and moved transformational options and the general mill levy off the 2026 list.

entry.title: Boulder: March 5, 2026 - Regular City Council Meeting (Boulder City Council)
entry.content:
The council heard extensive open comment on Flock Safety license-plate-reader cameras and on funding and future of the South Boulder Rec Center, declined to call up the Frontier Avenue concept plan, and approved the consent agenda (excluding item 3E, which was revised for staff direction) along with the 2026 board and commission appointments effective immediately for the Boulder Urban Renewal Authority. The meeting closed with a city staff presentation on affordable housing, prompting questions on cash-in-lieu, middle-income ownership, and the 15% affordable housing goal.

Most discussed: Boards & appointments, Affordable housing, Budget, Council governance, Housing, Parks & recreation

  • Open Comment: Flock Safety Cameras: Multiple residents urged the council to cancel or not renew the Flock Safety contract, citing ICE data-sharing concerns, racial profiling, security vulnerabilities, and reported misuse in other jurisdictions. Speakers asked for on-premises data storage alternatives and a surveillance-technology policy. Council members acknowledged the concerns and said staff is working on near-term contract decisions and a broader policy.
  • Open Comment: South Boulder Rec Center: Many speakers, including seniors, swimmers, parents, and a 10-year-old, urged funding to keep the South Boulder Rec Center open with its pool and gym. Speakers raised concerns about pool consolidation, aging infrastructure, and the 15-minute neighborhood goal. An engineering challenge and a petition for a retrofit commission were also presented.
  • Staff Responses and Council Comments on Open Comment: Staff said a April 9 study session will cover facilities funding and rec centers, and that Flock conversations are ongoing. The city attorney noted operations fall under the city manager, while council can set surveillance and privacy policy. Council members thanked speakers and encouraged continued civic participation, with speakers not selected being prioritized next meeting.
  • Consent Agenda and Item 3E Revision: The council amended the agenda to add item 3J on the external audit firm. Item 3E, concerning area three planning reserve guidance, was pulled for separate discussion and revised to make housing types broader than middle-income ownership. The remaining consent agenda items were approved unanimously.
  • Call-Up Check-In: Frontier Avenue Concept Plan: The council considered whether to call up a concept plan for redevelopment of 3550 and 3850 Frontier Avenue including an events venue, hotel, apartments, and commercial space. Council members noted zoning does not perfectly fit the mix of uses and expressed willingness to consider legislative changes later. The council declined to call up the project, with input to be given at site review.
  • Board and Commission Appointments 2026: A public hearing was held on 2026 board and commission appointments, with two speakers offering comments. Council members nominated candidates seat by seat, using straw votes and elimination rounds to narrow finalists. All appointments were approved unanimously, with Boulder Urban Renewal Authority appointments made effective immediately after a replacement motion.
  • Affordable Housing Review: Staff presented the current state of affordable housing, including the gap between stagnant area median income and rising home prices, Dr. Cog rental and ownership gaps, and the city's inclusionary housing outperformance at 37% of new development. Programs discussed include the affordable homeownership program, scattered-site acquisition, Boulder Mod, and the down payment assistance pilot. Council asked about cash-in-lieu economics, the 15% goal, unused $10 million voter-approved funds, and federal and vouchers impacts.
  • Closing Remarks and Community Announcement: Council members thanked staff for the affordable housing presentation and the city manager's office was encouraged to use the memo format as a model. A council member announced a community invitation to a Ramadan event at the mosque. The meeting was closed at 9:05 p.m.

entry.title: Boulder: February 19, 2026 Regular City Council Meeting
entry.content:
The Boulder City Council held its regular Thursday meeting, opening with extensive public comment, mostly from residents urging the city to keep the lap pool at the South Boulder Rec Center. The council unanimously approved the consent agenda and adopted resolution 1370 and ordinance 8734 to annex about 24 acres of city-owned Hogan-Pancost land, along with a land use map change for future parks and flood mitigation. Council also gave non-binding feedback on a concept plan for 281 apartments at 4880 Pearl Street, with members concerned about eroding industrial land.

Most discussed: Development projects, Parks & recreation, Zoning, Housing, Public comment, Homelessness

  • Open Comment and South Boulder Rec Center Pool: Residents, students, and families spoke during open comment, with most urging council to preserve the lap pool, gym, and cardio at the South Boulder Rec Center. Speakers cited its walkability, its role for Fairview swim team and schools, and a city petition with thousands of signatures.
