Other speakers raised concerns about foreign policy, a dog program, and homelessness and ambulance care. Council thanked the speakers, and staff said no decisions had been made on the rec center, which received $2 million in the 2025 budget, with study sessions planned for March and April.
  • Staff Responses to Open Comment: Staff responded to open comment on the city's new ambulance provider and an allegation of chemical sedation by the former provider, noting the related lawsuit was dismissed. Staff also said they would follow up on the Voice and Sight dog program concerns. Council members asked follow-up questions and thanked youth speakers and South Boulder residents.
  • Consent Agenda: Council considered consent agenda item 3, which included items 3A and 3B. Council members asked no questions, and a motion and second were made. The consent agenda was approved unanimously by roll call.
  • Annexation and Land Use Change for Hogan-Pancost Property: Council held a public hearing on annexing about 24 acres of city-owned Hogan-Pancost property and a portion of 55th Street right-of-way. Staff and Parks and Recreation described future flood mitigation and parks uses on the western portion, with open space preserved east of 55th Street. The annexation adopted resolution 1370 and ordinance 8734 with public zoning and RL2 zoning for the right-of-way, and the Boulder Valley Comprehensive Plan map change was approved. All votes were unanimous, and no public speakers were able to testify due to connection issues.
  • Concept Review for 4880 Pearl Street Residential Project: Council reviewed a concept plan for redeveloping the Boulder Storage site with four residential buildings containing 281 apartments and an 85,000-square-foot storage building. Staff said the General Industrial land use and IG zoning likely make residential inconsistent with the Boulder Valley Comprehensive Plan and East Boulder subcommunity plan, and raised contiguity and phasing concerns. Council members expressed concern about losing industrial land, the precedent for nearby parcels, and the need for more clarity on contiguity rules. No formal action was taken, and the applicant was asked to return with a revised concept.

entry.title: Boulder: February 12, 2026 - Boulder City Council Special Meeting
entry.content:
The special meeting covered a public hearing on whether the Area 3 Planning Reserve warranted further consideration of a service area expansion plan, a city manager matter on reconsidering comprehensive plan community change requests, a municipal court update, and a council community engagement discussion. Council voted 7-2 to find sufficient community need to continue exploring expansion, and directed staff to draft a guardrails resolution for consent agenda adoption at a future meeting.

Most discussed: Development projects, Zoning, Council governance, Crime & justice, Affordable housing, Wildfire

  • Area 3 Planning Reserve Service Area Expansion Need Determination: Staff presented a step two community needs assessment for the Area 3 Planning Reserve covering housing, fire storage, aging-related facilities, regional parkland, food systems, and renewable energy. Council questioned housing gap figures, parkland standards, water and wildfire resource impacts, staff capacity, and phasing. Planning board had voted 4-3 against continuing, and public speakers were split. Council approved the finding of sufficient need 7-2, with Wallik and Adams opposed.
  • Comprehensive Plan Community Change Requests Reconsideration: Staff reported that Boulder County commissioners supported reconsidering three land use requests and two policy requests that staff and the other bodies did not recommend advancing. Staff explained the policy edits already underway and why the requests were not recommended. Council raised no interest in reconsidering any of the requests, so no further action was taken.
  • Municipal Court 2025 Update and 2026 Work Plan: Judge Khan and Court Administrator Devon Kiss Kelly reviewed 2025 case filings, including rising traffic, photo enforcement, and criminal cases, and a rise in quality-of-life citations near CU. They described the community court, restorative programs, parking appeals, and the new public data dashboard. They also noted the Colorado Supreme Court's CAMP decision and pending public defender legislation. Council asked about traffic enforcement effectiveness, party-related enforcement, and the dashboard.
  • Council Community Engagement Options for 2026: Staff presented a menu of council engagement formats, including chats with council, council-initiated chats, office hours, community connectors events, and community and council forums. Council expressed interest in continuing chats and forums, with a nominated bike parking walk-and-talk downtown. Members discussed rotating topics and limiting labor-intensive events. Staff will take the feedback to the council engagement committee and return to council.

entry.title: Boulder: February 5, 2026 - City Council Regular Meeting
entry.content:
At its February 5, 2026 regular meeting, council heard extensive public comment, mostly from South Boulder residents urging the city to keep core amenities at the South Boulder Recreation Center, and then unanimously approved the Black History Month declaration and the consent agenda. Council adopted two East Boulder rezoning ordinances for a mixed-use project at 55th and Arapahoe and, after a straw poll, chose to pursue amendments to HB26-1001 (the Home Act) rather than take a flat position. Council also discussed the 2026 policy statement and followed up on its retreat priorities.

Most discussed: Housing, Regional & state relations, Zoning, Council governance, Parks & recreation, Budget

  • Opening, Announcements and Roll Call: Mayor Brockett opened the meeting and announced that the 2026 boards and commissions recruitment has closed, with virtual interviews running through February 13 and appointments scheduled for the March 5 meeting. Council completed a roll call confirming a quorum. Council then unanimously approved swapping agenda items 2A and 3 so that open comment came first.
  • Open Comment on the South Boulder Recreation Center: Many residents, including a nine-year-old, testified in person and online urging the city to keep the core amenities at the South Boulder Recreation Center, especially its lap pool and gym. Speakers cited a petition with about 3,000 signatures, use by the Fairview swim team and seniors, walkability, and emissions reduction. Several argued that the city has money for large office and East Boulder projects but not for South Boulder, and urged a ballot referral or a community vote.
  • Open Comment on HB26-1001 Home Act: Daniel Howard urged council to support HB26-1001 to address Colorado's housing shortage. He argued that the bill would let qualifying nonprofits, schools, churches and universities build on underused land through a faster standardized approval process. He noted that the bill still allows local inclusionary zoning, deed restrictions and height limits up to three stories or 45 feet.
  • Open Comment on Xcel Outages, Resilience Hubs and Coal Ash: Leslie Glustrom urged the city to plan for resilience hubs and interconnected microgrids rather than waiting for Xcel Energy to fix outages, and asked staff to develop a plan starting with three centers. Chris Hoffman thanked council for its letter to Xcel and urged gold-standard remediation of the Valmont coal ash site to avoid toxic dust exposure in Boulder.
  • Open Comment on Homeless Encampment Sweeps: Evan Rabbitz criticized council for approving more than $14 million for encampment sweeps and questioned the cost per unsheltered person. He also objected to council's position on the governor's zoning proposal and on divestment. His remarks focused on the city's homelessness approach and broader political concerns.
  • Open Comment on Towing Practices: Connor Robson petitioned council to address city towing practices after his car was towed from a street where he had parked during routine maintenance with 72-hour notice. He said the city's exclusive towing contractor charged $638 for under an hour of labor and that more than 20 cars were towed the same day. He asked the city to renegotiate allowable fees, require owner contact at tow time, or operate its own towing service.
  • Staff Responses on Recreation Centers and School Coordination: Parks and Recreation Director Ally Rhodes clarified that the city has not decided to close any facility and that council approved a $2 million investment at South Boulder in the 2025 budget. Staff said the long-term financial strategy and Fund Our Future conversations will return to council in March and May ahead of the 2027 budget and possible 2026 ballot items. Staff also said Boulder Valley School District does not offer pools, relies on nearby recreation centers for swim teams, and that emergency reunification is a benefit of proximity rather than a requirement.
  • Council Responses to Open Comment: Council members thanked the residents and youth who testified and noted that many city buildings are at the end of their lifespans with a roughly $400 million maintenance backlog. Council Member Adams asked staff about the status of county climate resilience hub grants and their alignment with the climate action plan update. Council Member Wallik clarified that he declined a petition because it did not allow for any design compromise, and the mayor said council shares the goal of an excellent South Boulder facility.
  • Black History Month Declaration: Council Member Adams read a declaration recognizing February 2026 as Black History Month, citing the 1926 origins of the observance and the theme of a century of Black history commemorations. The declaration highlighted Boulder figures and institutions, including the Boulder Blues baseball team and Second Baptist Church. Representatives of the CU Boulder Black Women's Alliance and Black Student Alliance accepted the declaration and spoke about their work.
  • Consent Agenda and Call-Up Check-Ins: Council unanimously approved consent agenda items 4A through 4C. During call-up check-ins, no member called up a landmark alteration certificate to demolish and rebuild an accessory building at 2408 (Mapleton Hill) or a request to construct a new primary building at 2439 Broadway, so both items stood approved.
  • East Boulder Rezoning Ordinances 8736 and 8737: Council held the second reading and public hearing on two rezoning ordinances for about 2.65 acres at 5501 and 5505 Arapahoe Avenue and adjacent rights-of-way, changing the zoning from BC1 to MU4 to support a form-based code redevelopment in East Boulder. Staff found the rezoning consistent with the comprehensive plan's mixed-use transit-oriented designation and the East Boulder subcommunity plan, and no written public comments were received. One resident opposed the rezoning as a density subsidy, while council members noted the irony of needing rezonings that the Title 9 update could address and Mark Wallik questioned the architecture produced by the form-based code. Council unanimously adopted both ordinances.
  • 2026 Policy Statement Updates: Heather Staer presented additions to the 2026 policy statement recommended by the Intergovernmental Affairs Committee, including human rights language, support for federally funded research jobs, food system and orphaned well cleanup, workforce housing, construction defects reform, coal ash mitigation, extreme fire day guidance, and limits on data center water and energy use. Council members asked whether local or state entities would determine excessive data center water use and asked that the item return to the IGA Committee. Council confirmed that several electrification and distributed generation positions are already covered in the existing policy statement.
  • HB26-1001 Home Act Discussion and Straw Poll: Staff summarized HB26-1001, which would require local governments to allow residential development on qualifying nonprofit, school, church, university and transit-agency properties of five acres or less through an administrative approval process, with limits on height and unit caps. Council questioned whether the bill preempts home rule, whether affordability is required, whether design or architecture can be regulated, and whether unincorporated county parcels are eligible. Council straw polled and chose to pursue amendments, with a majority supporting an amend position and a smaller group favoring oppose unless amended. The amendments requested include excluding unincorporated county land, limiting nonprofit eligibility, applying local height standards, requiring a demonstrated housing need, and requiring consistency with the comprehensive plan, though the comprehensive plan request was later withdrawn as a likely poison pill.
  • Council Retreat Priorities Follow-Up: Matt Chasanoff presented staff's project charters for council's retreat priorities, including bicycle security and theft reduction, wildfire home hardening and mitigation analysis, exploring local tip credit authority beginning in 2027, power resiliency with Xcel Energy, and sister city program updates. Staff noted that Title 9 rewrite was added as a caveated item if time allows and that a bike parking capital project will not occur in 2026 due to limited resources. Council asked for prioritized, action-oriented wildfire recommendations rather than academic analysis, and asked staff to bring a tip credit ordinance by June 2026 with a check-in in April. Council also requested public safety and agricultural updates, and staff committed to follow up on e-bike regulation research.
  • Closing Comments on Downtown Parking and ENCAR Property: Council Member Tara Mates raised concern about high downtown parking costs and said she asked staff to research parking pricing trends after council approved a 50-cent increase in the budget. Council Member Adams asked for a frequently asked questions document on ownership of the ENCAR property, and staff said they are reviewing archives and may need executive session for legal advice. Mayor Brockett then closed the meeting at 9:11 p.m.

entry.title: Boulder: January 22, 2026 - City Council Special Meeting
entry.content:
The Boulder City Council read a Holocaust Remembrance Day declaration, passed a consent agenda unanimously, and unanimously adopted Ordinance 8731, which modernizes city purchasing rules and raises the informal bid threshold to $100,000. The council also approved, with one request removed and two added back, the list of community change requests for the Boulder Valley Comprehensive Plan update, and directed staff to return with a commercial-focused metro district policy framework for adoption in April. Council closed the meeting after discussing a volunteer for the regional homelessness working group.

Most discussed: Zoning, Economic development, Development projects, Taxes & fees, Housing, Council governance

  • International Holocaust Remembrance Day Declaration: Mayor Pro Tem Winer read a declaration designating January 27, 2026 as International Holocaust Remembrance Day. The declaration recounts the Nazi persecution and murder of Jews, Roma, disabled people, and others. It condemns antisemitism, hatred, and bigotry in all forms and pledges solidarity with the Jewish community. The declaration was presented as a ceremonial item.
  • Consent Agenda (Items 3A-3G): Council took up the consent agenda, covering items 3A through 3G. Council members commented on item G, a letter to Xcel Energy setting out the city's expectations after the city declined an offer in 2025. Staff were praised for the draft letter. The consent agenda passed unanimously by roll call.
  • Ordinance 8731: Purchasing Procedures Update: Staff presented updates to Chapter 2-8 of the Boulder Revised Code to modernize purchasing, the first update since 1997. Key changes include raising the informal bid threshold from $50,000 to $100,000, allowing alternative construction delivery methods, clarifying piggyback contracting and bid rejection, strengthening equity and sustainability language, and creating a business opportunity program for small, minority, and women-owned businesses. A public speaker raised divestment from Israel, which the mayor ruled off topic. Council adopted the ordinance unanimously on second reading.
  • Boulder Valley Comprehensive Plan Community Change Requests: Staff presented 34 community change requests received between August and October 2025 and recommended which should advance to further analysis in the draft plan due March 2. Council heard from several residents opposing request 10 on Sue Drive, which was removed from the list by a 7-2 straw vote. Council added requests 26 and 27, on wildfire mitigation and agricultural water use, back into the list after staff had recommended against them. Council then approved the amended list unanimously, with staff to evaluate the requests further and report back in the draft plan.
  • Metro District Policy Framework: Staff presented recommendations for a policy framework regulating commercial-focused metropolitan districts, targeting an ordinance and model service plan for adoption in April ahead of a possible November 2026 ballot cycle. Key recommendations include limiting residential to about 10% of floor area, a 50 debt mill levy cap with a combined cap, provisions for operations and maintenance and fees, third-party certification of developer debt, and periodic reviews. Council asked about tax burdens compared with other Front Range communities, anti-displacement review, and protections for the city in interactions with other special districts. Council affirmed staff to move forward with the framework.
  • Boulder County Regional Homelessness Working Group Vacancy: The mayor noted a vacancy on the Boulder County Elected Officials Regional Working Group on Homelessness, previously held by Lauren Folkart. Tara declined the permanent seat, and Tina volunteered to serve as alternate. Matt and Mark were both interested in the permanent seat and agreed to resolve it offline. The appointment is expected to be finalized on consent at a future meeting.

entry.title: Boulder: January 8, 2026 - Boulder City Council Special Meeting (with Downtown Commercial District, Nwood Metropolitan District, and annexation/ordinance hearings)
entry.content:
The council heard extensive open comment on Flock Safety cameras, PSPS outages, proportional representation, and other topics, then received a staff recap of the December wind and power shut-off response. It approved the consent agenda including the Sundance Institute governing agreement, approved Downtown Commercial District Resolution 319 for Sundance incentives, and passed the 915 Fifth Street annexation ordinances. It also amended and passed Ordinance 8721 on landscaping, water conservation, and wildfire resilience for a third reading, declined to call up an Arapahoe Avenue form-based code project, and discussed 2026 committee appointments.

Most discussed: Public comment, Climate & sustainability, Flock cameras, Water & flooding, Development projects, Surveillance & privacy

  • Open Comment Period: Residents spoke on a range of topics including surface parking at Engineering Center, Flock Safety camera vulnerabilities and data sharing, CU student move-out waste diversion, Eco Visits for wildlife, council decorum and Caterpillar divestment, proportional representation, Excel Energy and a sustainable energy utility, and rec center lap pool concerns. Staff and council responded briefly to the comments, including follow-ups on resilience hubs, closed captioning, and Flock data policy.
  • PSPS and Windstorm Response Summary: Staff presented a recap of the city's response to the December public safety power shut-off and windstorm, including emergency operations center activation, increased fire and police call volume, and generator support for water plants and intersections. Around 60% of the community lost power, and no serious injuries or fires were reported. A virtual town hall and an after-action report are planned, and the city will work with Excel and the PUC on future shut-off planning. Council thanked staff for the response.
  • Consent Agenda and Sundance Institute Agreement: The council approved the consent agenda items, with item 4D removed earlier, including the governing agreement with the Sundance Institute to host the Sundance Film Festival from 2027 through 2036. Staff explained the agreement includes parking revenue sharing and reporting terms. Council members raised concerns about community benefit tracking and the lack of an equity analysis, and the consent agenda passed unanimously.
  • Downtown Commercial District Board Actions: The council convened as the Downtown Commercial District board and approved Resolution 319, which sets incentives for the Sundance Institute and authorizes the general manager to negotiate and execute a lease. A council member asked whether the parking revenue split depends on current or future rates, and staff confirmed it is based on festival-period pricing with a 50/50 split. The board then adjourned and reconvened as the city council.
  • Call-Up of Arapahoe Avenue Form-Based Code Review: The council considered calling up a form-based code review for a five-story mixed-use building with 300 dwelling units at 5501 and 5505 Arapahoe Avenue. Some members said the form-based code produced a poor aesthetic result, but others stressed keeping the administrative track predictable and not punishing applicants who followed the rules. The motion to call up the project failed 4 to 5, so the project was not called up.
  • Nwood Metropolitan District Budget Amendment: Staff presented a supplemental appropriation of about $7,400 for the 2025 Nwood Metropolitan District budget to cover dissolution-related expenses that exceeded the original budget, and noted an accounting error that created a negative fund balance. The public hearing drew comments from one resident about the cost. Council then adopted Resolution 4 unanimously and reconvened as the city council.
  • 915 Fifth Street Annexation and Zoning: Council held the second reading on the series annexation of the 1.294-acre property at 915 Fifth Street, with initial RE zoning. Staff recommended against the planning board's proposed 4,000-square-foot floor area limit because it was inconsistent with past annexations, and the applicant did not want that restriction. Council adopted Resolution 1364, Resolution 1365, and Ordinances 8728, 8729, and 8730, and the water conservancy district consent, all unanimously.
  • Ordinance 8721: Landscaping, Water Conservation, and Wildfire Resilience: Staff presented revisions to landscape code and wildland urban interface requirements, moving technical standards into a city manager landscape manual, updating non-functional turf rules to comply with state law, and clarifying wildfire hardening rules. Changes from earlier council feedback included removing tree removal requirements, restoring existing trigger thresholds, allowing daytime watering in winter, and easing weed barrier restrictions. Council amended and passed the ordinance, which will move to third reading.
  • 2026 Council Committee Appointments: Staff walked council through vacancies on boards, committees, and sister city liaison roles, with members volunteering for Boulder County Consortium of Cities, Mile High Flood District, Boards and Commissions Committee, Charter Committee, Financial Strategy Committee, and intergovernmental affairs. Members also swapped sister city liaisons and Taisha offered to give up the Audit Committee seat. Council asked staff to look into moving the ARAB seat to staff and to clarify the county homelessness working group appointment, with a January 13 deadline for recommendations.

entry.title: Boulder: Boulder City Council Study Session - October 12, 2023
entry.content:
Council reviewed three items: a Camp (Chautauqua/Shanahan-area) trailhead access management program update, the implementation process for East Boulder subcommunity plan zoning and form-based code, and a discussion of supporting Boulder County ballot measure 1A for open space sales and use tax extension. Council generally supported continuing Camp with planned changes and a feasibility study of direct transit access, asked staff to be cautious about raising fees on residents, and directed staff to refine form-based code review and bring back zoning recommendations; Council unanimously supported measure 1A, with a consent item planned for the next business meeting.

Most discussed: Zoning, Parking, Development projects, Housing, Transit, Open space

  • Camp Trailhead Access Management Program Update: Staff recommended continuing the Camp park-to-park shuttle and paid parking program during its traditional summer season with planned changes such as micromobility, B-cycle station, signage and routing updates. Staff also proposed possible modifications including performance-based pricing, a commuter permit program for employees, and using parking revenue for TDM benefits. Staff requested a feasibility study of direct transit or microtransit access beyond the current park-and-ride model. Council members generally supported continuing Camp and exploring the feasibility study, but expressed caution about raising parking costs for city residents and the equity of access.
  • East Boulder Subcommunity Plan Zoning and Form-Based Code: Staff presented the process update on implementing zoning recommendations from the East Boulder subcommunity plan, including a rezoning strategy and a review of the form-based code applied to Boulder Junction and Alpine-Balsam projects. Staff noted the code aims to deliver walkable neighborhoods but has drawn concerns about cost, design variety, and frequent discretionary call-ups. Council asked that feedback from the development community and planning board be incorporated, that discretionary review be limited, that rules be reassessed, and that roof variability and more iconic buildings be allowed. Staff will return with draft recommendations in a couple of months.
  • Support for Boulder County Ballot Measure 1A: Council discussed supporting Boulder County ballot measure 1A, a 0.5% sales tax for open space purchase and maintenance. Councilmember Brockett raised the item and asked for council's temperature on a position of support. Council unanimously indicated support, and staff was directed to request that the item be placed on the consent agenda at the next business meeting.

entry.title: Boulder: Boulder City Council Meeting - Thursday October 5, 2023 (Regular Meeting)
entry.content:
The council opened with a Indigenous Peoples' Day declaration and National Domestic Violence Month proclamation, then heard extensive open comment on rowing reservoir fees, pollinator gardens, bike path lighting, traffic safety, policing, housing, and budget concerns. It approved the consent agenda including a prairie dog management update and a police oversight ordinance review, annexed a 2.27-acre property at 30333 Street as RL1, and adopted first readings of the 2024 budget with added funding for pavement management, underpass lighting, and community connectors. Council also directed staff to scope a 25-person safe outdoor space pilot.

Most discussed: Budget, Transportation, Public comment, Taxes & fees, Homelessness, Parks & recreation

  • Indigenous Peoples' Day Declaration: Council Member Wier presented a declaration recognizing October 9, 2023 as Indigenous Peoples' Day. It acknowledges the history of violence against Indigenous peoples in Boulder, including the Sand Creek Massacre, and references the city's 2016 resolution and ongoing work with tribal nations.
  • National Domestic Violence Month Declaration: Mayor Brockett presented a declaration designating October as National Domestic Violence Month. The statement highlights prevalence statistics and local resources, including the Safehouse Progressive Alliance for Nonviolence and the National Domestic Violence Hotline. The council urged community participation in observances.
  • Open Comment on Rowing Reservoir Fees and Hours: Multiple rowing club representatives from CU, Boulder Community Rowing, and Colorado Junior Crew described sharp increases in reservoir after-hours fees and asked for earlier opening hours. Parks and Recreation staff responded that adult user groups must cover direct costs, that water quality is a priority, and that fees would be set under a new policy with no increase above 10 percent.
  • Open Comment on Pollinator Gardens, Bike Path Lighting, and Traffic Safety: Residents asked the city to incorporate pollinator gardens into transportation project design, improve nighttime lighting on the Boulder Creek path between 30th Street and Foothills Parkway, and convert the 23rd and Bluff Street intersection to a four-way stop. A resident also reported poor road conditions on Foothills Parkway for cyclists.
  • Open Comment on Policing and Community Concerns: A resident criticized the police department for redacting a use-of-force case from public records and alleged the NAACP was pressured over complaints about a deputy chief. Staff stated the city stands behind Deputy Chief Redfern, whose testimony is part of a trial of Aurora officers, and said the city does not believe any wrongdoing occurred.
  • Open Comment on Housing, Homelessness, and Environmental Concerns: Speakers raised concerns about the city's camping ban and enforcement against homeless residents, the proposed day shelter, and the impact of rising rents. Others called for the city to honor Elder Oak's environmental advocacy, and a speaker spoke against a proposed drug-treatment facility while urging the council to decline state funding.
  • Historic Preservation and Civic Area Phase Two Concerns: Patrick Oror of Historic Boulder raised concerns that the Civic Area historic district application was not mentioned in reports on Civic Area Phase Two and that the finance department proposed selling several central Boulder buildings that may be historic. Staff said these issues are known and agreed to provide information on the buildings in question.
  • Open Comment on Landmarks Process and Theft Incident: Lynn Seagull criticized the Landmarks Design Review Committee's fast-track approval of a large addition and said her bag and $360 were stolen from the municipal building lobby. Staff said investigators are working with her and the city wants to make her whole.
  • Open Comment on Road Safety for State Highway 93: Matthew Hannah asked the council to advocate for changing the merge direction on southbound State Highway 93 so that lanes merge from left to right. He argued the change would encourage drivers to keep right and reduce unsafe merging on the curved uphill segment.
  • Open Comment on Rowing Access and Reservoir Opening Hours: Bridget Hogan, a parent of a rower, described how the Colorado Junior Crew program would be jeopardized if after-hours reservoir fees doubled. She asked the council and reservoir staff to partner with the volunteer program to provide sustainable access.
  • Staff Response to Open Comment and Reservoir Fee Discussion: Staff said the city would investigate the bike path lighting and reservoir fee concerns, noted that the Transportation director was listening to transportation comments, and confirmed that a staff investigation into the stolen bag is underway. Parks and Recreation director Ali Rhodes explained the cost-recovery rationale for adult rowing user groups, stated that no fee doubling is planned, and said fee schedules would be included in an information item.
  • Consent Agenda Items 3A-3G: The consent agenda included an open space prairie dog management update with Council approval for changes to lethal control and burrow disturbance limits, the police oversight ordinance update, a letter to county commissioners, and an employee evaluation process for the city manager and city attorney. Council passed the consent agenda unanimously, with Mayor Pro Tem Wallik voting no on item G.
  • Annexation of 30333 Street Property: Council held a public hearing and adopted Resolution 1333 setting findings of fact and conclusions for annexing a 2.27-acre property at 30333 Street with an initial zoning of RL1. Council also passed Ordinance 8582 approving the annexation. The annexation agreement includes preservation of Area 3 under a 1981 scenic easement and an inclusionary housing payment requirement.
  • 2024 Budget Public Hearing and First Readings: Staff presented the $148 million all-funds 2024 recommended budget, including a $16.1 million general fund and a $141.4 million Capital Improvement Program. Council approved first readings of Ordinances 8595, 8596, 8597, and 8598 with amendments adding $500,000 for pavement management, $30,000 for underpass lighting, $10,000 for Community Connectors, and reallocating travel funding. Ordinance 8598 on non-residential fees was introduced without changes.
  • Council Proposed Budget Changes: Council discussed proposed changes including increased funding for the Central Area General Improvement District ambassador program funded through the kid fund, $10,000 for Community Connectors, pavement management and underpass lighting increases, reallocation of Safe and Managed Public Spaces funding, and deferral of FAA projects. Council did not support redirecting most Safe and Managed Public Spaces funding but directed staff to study additional funding for housing supports.
  • Pavement Management and Road Maintenance: Transportation staff reported that pavement conditions have deteriorated due to climate-driven freeze-thaw cycles and a wet summer. Council voted to add $500,000 in one-time funding for pavement management, with staff noting that Staffing and contractor availability limit reactive pothole repairs. Council members expressed interest in a longer-term funding strategy for road maintenance next year.
  • Underpass Lighting Improvements: Staff explained that 12 underpasses are lit 24/7 at an annual cost of about $27,000 and that extending lighting to all underpasses would cost roughly $30,000 more per year. Options discussed included painting underpasses to ease visual transitions and increasing inspections. Council approved an additional $30,000 for underpass lighting from the transportation fund.
  • Safe Outdoor Space Pilot Direction: Council voted to direct staff to develop a pilot for a sanctioned encampment of approximately 25 people at the bronze level of service, funded from savings in the day shelter operations budget. Staff will return with cost estimates, location options, and an implementation plan, and will consider safe outdoor parking as well. Council voted to approve the notice of motion, with a majority in favor.
  • Council Member Updates and Closing Remarks: Council Member Matt Benjamin announced he has been asked to chair the Colorado Municipal League Policy Committee from October through March. Council Member Rachel Friend requested a future conversation on bike safety and e-bike conflicts. The meeting adjourned at 10:51 p.m.

entry.title: Boulder: Boulder City Council Study Session - September 28, 2023 (Municipal Court Overview, Police Department Update, and Homelessness Programs Update)
entry.content:
Council received three presentations: a Municipal Court overview covering its problem-solving approach, Community Court, FastTrack student cases, jail booking constraints and high-utilizer efforts; a Police Department update on rising violent and property crime, fentanyl-driven overdoses, significant incidents and community engagement; and a Housing and Human Services homelessness update on new programs including local vouchers, Building Home, a rest and recuperation center, safe outdoor space options and winter shelter planning. Council members asked for follow-up data and a future conversation on Community Court, and by consensus asked staff to bring a formal item on exploring alternative sheltering, including safe outdoor spaces, with budget implications to be considered.

Most discussed: Homelessness, Crime & justice, Police, Budget, Council governance, Legal & litigation

  • Municipal Court Overview and Community Court: Judge Conan described the court's problem-solving philosophy, administrative changes, and the new live-stream requirement. She explained the FastTrack process for student quality-of-life violations, which emphasizes quick court dates and restorative justice with CU. Council members questioned how prosecutors choose between Community Court and traditional court, and staff agreed to provide the eligibility criteria and a fuller explanation in a hotline post. Jail booking standards and the 48-hour PR bond rule were also discussed as constraints.
  • Municipal Court Questions and Follow-Up: Council asked about longer jail sentences, which the judge said are rare and used only as a last resort after programs are refused. Questions addressed whether community court is reserved for unhoused people, and council requested data comparing outcomes and recidivism for those who use and do not use Community Court. Council members also asked about trespass charges, consequences, and the need for sober living and transitional housing after jail. A future conversation with the sheriff and prosecutor was requested.
  • Police Department Crime Trends and Overdoses: Chief Harold presented five-year crime data showing rising simple and aggravated assaults and menacing, with robberies down and property theft up, while motor vehicle theft is down 48% since 2020. Drug and narcotics violations are up 79%, and downtown and University Hill account for a large share of overdoses and fatal overdoses, mostly involving fentanyl. Staff noted that officers are administering Narcan several times daily.
  • Police Problem Locations and Significant Incidents: Deputy Chief Redfern reported on problem-location work at the library and the Circle K at 14th and Canyon, where directed patrols reduce crime when present. The department reviewed significant incidents including a fatal officer-involved shooting, a child homicide, a stolen-car standoff, two fatal motorcycle crashes with speed as a factor, a downtown stabbing with a released suspect, a Central Park drug operation, and a serious Hill burglary series. Council was told community outreach included Pride, a youth academy, an international policing conference, and K9 Astro's certification.
  • Police Council Questions on Jail Capacity, Motor Vehicle Theft and Violence: Council asked why jail capacity is strained, and staff said the jail is back at the pandemic-era cap of about 490 with a backlog of people awaiting competency trials. Discussion covered the impact of released defendants and an inability to hold people awaiting trial. Council asked how motor vehicle theft fell, and staff cited education, state investigators, stings and cameras. Council also raised concerns about hate crimes, domestic violence, human trafficking, drug combinations such as xylazine, and staffing needs, and staff agreed to send data.
  • Homelessness Services Update and Point-in-Time Count: Housing and Human Services presented a summer point-in-time count showing similar totals of about 350 single adults in winter and summer, and about 25 monthly exits from homelessness in Boulder. Staff described new programs including the local voucher program, shelter unit acquisitions, the Building Home program, a planned rest and recuperation center funded by a $2 million state grant, the High Utilizer partnership, and the Day Services Center, which lost its site but gained state funding for expanded services. The presentation also covered coordinated entry, racial equity data, the Outreach team, and a $11.6 million 2024 investment.
  • Homelessness Council Questions and Follow-Up: Council asked about staff support hours for newly housed individuals, the Mental Health Partners acute care campus, shelter bed utilization averaging about 10 unused beds per night, and whether a council seat on the Homeless Solutions Committee is possible. Questions also covered the evidence for sanctioned encampments and the funding for new services. Staff agreed to provide data on shelter bed usage, family homelessness and shelter capacity trends.
  • Alternative Sheltering and Safe Outdoor Spaces Direction: Staff presented options for alternative sheltering, including safe outdoor spaces and pallet shelters, with cost estimates based largely on Denver and noting that infrastructure and staffing drive costs. Council members expressed interest in further exploration, with some preferring incremental shelter bed expansion or indoor options. Council discussed funding sources and the budget implications and agreed to schedule a formal item to bring the question back.
  • Council Direction and Closing Remarks: Council reviewed the requested direction on the homelessness program ideas and generally supported the new programs, with the majority supporting further exploration of alternative sheltering. Council decided to bring a formal item at a later meeting and tie funding questions to the budget discussion. Staff explained infrastructure needs for City-owned sites and thanked council and the community partners.

entry.title: Boulder: Boulder City Council Regular Meeting - September 21, 2023
entry.content:
The Council opened with proclamations for Hispanic Heritage Month and Energy Efficiency Day, then heard extensive open comment and consent agenda items. The main actions were approving amendments to the Transit Village Area Plan (Boulder Junction Phase 2) and its Comprehensive Plan summary, and amending Ordinance 8599 on zoning for affordable and modest-size housing, with several changes deferred to phase two. The Council also discussed a letter endorsing county housing support, with a directive to bring a formal endorsement back later.

Most discussed: Affordable housing, Zoning, Development projects, Housing, Parking, Public comment

  • Hispanic Heritage Month and Energy Efficiency Day Declarations: Council presented a proclamation recognizing Hispanic Heritage Month from September 15 to October 15, with interpreters and community members speaking in Spanish and English. Council then presented an Energy Efficiency Day declaration for October 2023, urging residents to support clean energy goals.
  • Open Comment Period: Eight in-person speakers and one virtual speaker addressed Council on topics including library building disposition, a Museum of Boulder exhibit, police monitor and homelessness near Central Park, architectural preservation, potty training facilities, a Landmarks Design Review Committee demolition, and a 28th and J housing project. Staff responded to several concerns, including the Central Park incident and the housing project.
  • Consent Agenda and Call-Up Check-In: Council approved consent agenda items 3A through 3F unanimously by roll call. No council member called up the Life Sciences site review at 3825 Walnut Street, so it proceeded without a call-up.
  • Boulder Junction Phase 2 Transit Village Area Plan Amendments: Staff presented amendments to the 2007 Transit Village Area Plan covering land use, transportation connections, and urban design for the Boulder Junction Phase 2 area. Council discussed mixed-use transit-oriented development versus mixed-use industrial zoning, anti-displacement strategies for small businesses, and retail sizing. Council approved both motions unanimously, including the staff recommendation not to add the planning board's office restriction.
  • Ordinance 8599: Zoning for Affordable and Modest-Size Housing: Staff presented second reading amendments to the land use code to ease density, parking, and subdivision rules, aiming to increase middle housing and modest-size units. Council discussed site review exemptions, efficiency living unit use review, floor area bonuses, and rmx-1 rezoning, deferring several items to a future phase. Council amended and passed the ordinance unanimously, with a third reading expected as a consent item.
  • Letter to County Commissioners on Housing Ballot Measure: Council member Benjamin proposed a letter to County Commissioners endorsing a proposed affordable and attainable housing tax, requesting investment in permanent supportive housing with wraparound services and transitional housing. Council generally supported sending the letter, with a formal endorsement resolution to follow through a future request.

entry.title: Boulder: September 14, 2023 - Boulder City Council Study Session
entry.content:
Council gave staff direction on the intergovernmental agreement with the Boulder Public Library District, including a hybrid trustee appointment process with a three-year check-in and a longer-term lease option with a district-only termination right at five-year intervals. Council then reviewed the $514.8 million recommended 2024 budget, which covers community connector feedback, new investments, capital projects, and unfunded needs. Councilmembers were asked to submit proposed changes by September 25 ahead of the October 5 first reading.

Most discussed: Budget, Regional & state relations, Legal & litigation, Council governance, Equity & civil rights, Boards & appointments

  • Library District IGA Background and Assumptions: Staff reviewed the history of forming the Boulder Public Library District, including the 2018 library master plan and the 2022 voter-approved district formation. Staff noted that the city will no longer treat library services as a core city function and that the district will be governed by its own trustees. Many transition issues such as IT and employment were described as technical, while appointment and property questions were flagged for council policy feedback.
  • Library Trustee Appointment Process: Staff presented three options for selecting library trustees: continuing the joint council and county committee model, delegating selection to the trustees, or a hybrid with non-voting trustee participation. Council discussed reviewing the approach in three years, which aligned with staff's recommendation. Council members then gave a unanimous straw poll favoring the hybrid approach with a three-year check-in.
  • Library Property Disposition and Lease Term: Staff outlined options for city-owned library buildings, including conveyance, leases, or a mix where the city keeps the land at the main library. Council straw polls favored leasing the branch libraries over transferring them, and the city also discussed a right of reversion. Members debated lease length, with trustees preferring a long-term lease, and eventually supported a 20 to 30 year lease with a district-only termination option at five-year intervals. Staff were directed to offer this as a possible negotiation point rather than a requirement.
  • 2024 Budget Overview and Revenue Outlook: The city manager and CFO introduced the $514.8 million 2024 recommended budget, emphasizing constrained resources and sustainability, equity, and resilience goals. Staff projected sales and use tax about 2.3 percent lower than prior models, citing slowing retail and inflation. Property assessments rose about 32 percent, with Proposition HH on the November ballot and a possible property tax cap being monitored. The general fund includes a one-time $13 million repayment expected from the Library District.
  • Community Connector Budget Engagement: Community connectors Jamal Gilmore and Lenora Cooper presented feedback gathered over several months from historically excluded communities. Top priorities included housing affordability, financial security and economic opportunity, and advancing racial equity. Mental health and youth opportunities emerged as the biggest shifts in community needs. Council thanked the connectors and expressed interest in continued partnership, one-on-one meetings, and expanded engagement in future budgets.
  • Key Budget Investments and Capital Improvement Program: Staff highlighted major investments including behavioral health response programs, $31.8 million for affordable housing including the Ponderosa stabilization project, and wildfire mitigation grants. New investments also covered living wage increases and collective bargaining agreements for city employees. The six-year capital program totals about $900 million, with the Western City Campus project and debt service increases to fund it. Other capital projects include East Boulder Community Center retrofits, new fire stations, and Pearl Street Mall improvements.
  • Operating Investments by Goal Area and Unfunded Needs: Staff reviewed operating investments across goal areas such as environmental sustainability, livability, safety, healthy community, and economic vitality. Staff acknowledged about $30 million in general fund unfunded needs, including facility maintenance, affordable housing, fire master plan implementation, and parks maintenance. A citywide strategic plan and a long-term financial strategy were proposed to guide future prioritization.
  • Council Budget Review Process and Questions: Staff explained the review timeline, with council change requests due September 25 and a first reading on October 5. Councilmembers asked about snow and ice removal, pothole repairs, the South Boulder Rec Center, Pilot program evaluation, and unspent day services funds. Council emphasized that any requested additions must identify offsetting reductions to maintain a zero-sum budget. Councilmembers praised staff for the budget work and thanked the community connectors before the meeting closed at 9:50 pm.

entry.title: Boulder: September 7, 2023 - Boulder City Council Regular Meeting
entry.content:
The Boulder City Council opened with declarations (flood anniversary, National Voter Registration Day, Suicide Prevention Month) and open comment, then approved the consent agenda, including a resolution supporting LGBTQ+ access to public accommodations. The council heard extensive public testimony and accepted the Reimagine Policing Plan and disbanded its subcommittee unanimously. It also received a staff update on inclusionary housing changes, with direction to pursue cash-in-lieu restructuring, reduced on-site requirements, and a possible linkage fee study.

Most discussed: Police, Affordable housing, Public comment, Emergency management, Budget, Housing

  • Declarations and Announcements: Council read declarations recognizing the 10th anniversary of the 2013 Front Range flood, National Voter Registration Day on September 19, and National Suicide Prevention Month. Rise Against Suicide's Jenna Carr and Lauren spoke in appreciation of the recognition. Staff also announced the What's Up Boulder event and the Better Public Meetings scorecard.
  • Open Comment Public Testimony: Residents spoke on the proposed Boulder Airport closure, police oversight and officer conduct, the hill commercial area liquor regulations, and bear activity and trash in the University Hill area. Other speakers raised South Boulder maintenance concerns and homelessness camp proposals. Council members and staff responded and committed to follow-ups.
  • Consent Agenda: Council approved the consent agenda items 3a through 3i unanimously. Item 3h concerned a planning matter with a second reading scheduled for September 21 and possible third reading. Item 3i was Resolution 1339 supporting LGBTQ+ people's access to goods, services, and public accommodations without discrimination in light of the 303 Creative decision.
  • Call-Up Check-In for 1345 28th Street: Council considered calling up a site review for three student housing apartment buildings at 1345 28th Street. No member requested a call-up, so the item proceeded with planning board review.
  • Reimagine Policing Plan Public Hearing: Chief Maris Harold, Wendy Schwarz, and Robin Engel of the National Policing Institute presented the Reimagine Policing Plan, which emphasizes problem-solving policing, holistic governance, staffing aligned to the ICMA rule of 60, and accountability metrics. Staff noted that the funding requests would come through future budget cycles. Council and speakers largely supported the plan, though some residents raised concerns about downtown crime and staffing levels.
  • Public Testimony on Reimagine Policing: Speakers representing business groups, neighborhood associations, and residents voiced strong support for the plan, citing crime on Pearl Street and in the downtown area. Some speakers called for more police staffing and criticized council decisions and the police oversight panel. Others urged equity and community engagement in implementation.
  • Council Discussion and Vote on Reimagine Policing: Council members praised the community engagement process and the work of the subcommittee. Several members stressed that the plan is a roadmap requiring ongoing implementation and accountability. Council then approved a motion to accept the plan and disband the subcommittee by roll call vote, unanimously.
  • Inclusionary Housing Program Update: Staff presented proposed updates to the inclusionary housing program, including moving cash-in-lieu to a per-square-foot basis, reducing the on-site for-sale requirement from 25% to 15%, and exploring a Nexus study for a linkage fee on demolitions and large additions. Kaiser Marston's feasibility analysis found developers consistently choose cash-in-lieu over on-site units. Council members expressed concern about trading on-site middle-income units for more off-site rental units, but supported the code cleanups and continued analysis.

entry.title: Boulder: Boulder City Council Study Session - August 24, 2023
entry.content:
The council held a study session covering three items: Community Broadband (staff presented research on three potential paths forward, including a municipal utility, a public-private partnership, and a backbone lease, with council asking for more information on take rates, costs, and lease terms before a future public hearing), the Boulder Airport community conversation (council requested more information on FAA grant obligations and closure feasibility before staff returns in early 2024), and minimum wage (staff reported on regional efforts; council debated accelerating to a 2024 increase, and by a 5-4 split directed staff to stay with the 2025 regional timeline). No formal decisions were made on broadband or the airport.

Most discussed: Transportation, Regional & state relations, Labor & wages, Public comment, Technology & broadband, Economic development

  • Community Broadband: Staff presented research on internet access and affordability, noting over 99 percent of households have wired broadband but only about 36 percent have fiber, with limited provider choice. Three potential paths were outlined: a municipal internet utility (estimated at $218 million, requiring about $268 million in debt and roughly $14 million annual general fund subsidy), a public-private partnership, and a non-exclusive backbone lease, which staff recommended as the lowest-risk and fastest option. Council asked follow-up questions on take rates, lease conditions, equity of build-out, and financing, and staff will return with more information at a future public hearing.
  • Boulder Airport Community Conversation: Staff presented results of community engagement on the future of the Boulder Municipal Airport, including questionnaires, open houses, and a community working group, and four draft scenarios ranging from enhanced maintenance to decommissioning and redeveloping the site. Community input emphasized noise, leaded fuel, and safety concerns, with near-term action items identified. Council discussed FAA grant assurances and closure obligations, with the FAA indicating closure would be difficult, and asked for more legal and factual clarity before returning in early 2024.
  • Minimum Wage Regional Effort: Staff updated council on the regional minimum wage working group with Longmont, Louisville, Lafayette, and Erie, and on Boulder County's decision to pursue a 15 percent increase effective January 2024. Staff noted that accelerating Boulder's timeline would require pausing regional collaboration and conducting a shorter engagement process without an economic analysis. Council members debated the tradeoffs between responding to urgent community need and maintaining regional partnership, and by a 5-4 vote directed staff to stay with the regional 2025 timeline.
